## What it says
For a negative integer $a$, the rank-one lattice $\langle a\rangle$ has signature $(0, 0, 1)$: no positive direction, no null direction and one negative direction.

- `(ha : a < 0)`: the hypothesis `ha` that the integer $a$ is negative; $a$ itself is an implicit argument, read off from `ha`.
- The conclusion: `(rankOne a).signature = (0, 0, 1)`. Here `rankOne a` is the integral lattice $\langle a\rangle$, the integers inside $\mathbb{Q}$ with the form $B(x, y) = axy$, and `signature` is the triple $(n_+, n_0, n_-)$ of an integral lattice: the numbers of positive, null and negative directions of its form.

This is the standard computation. For $a < 0$ the form $ax^2$ is negative at every nonzero $x$, so the line is a single negative direction: $\langle a\rangle$ is negative definite of rank one, of signature $(0, 1)$ in the usual pair $(n_+, n_-)$, written here with the null count in the middle.

## What it says
Given an integral lattice $L$ in a rational vector space $V$, a basis of the lattice over $\mathbb{Z}$ is also a basis of $V$ over $\mathbb{Q}$; `rationalBasis` is that $\mathbb{Q}$-basis, built from the basis of $L$ that Lean chooses.

- `[AddCommGroup V] [Module ℚ V]`: $V$ is a vector space over the rationals $\mathbb{Q}$ (an additive commutative group with a $\mathbb{Q}$-module structure); $V$ is any type.
- `(L : IntegralLattice V)`: an integral lattice $L$ in $V$: a subgroup `L.carrier` of $V$ that is a full lattice, finitely generated and spanning $V$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, with a symmetric rational bilinear form on $V$ that is integral on it.
- The value is a basis of $V$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ indexed by `Module.Free.ChooseBasisIndex ℤ ↥L.carrier`. It takes `Module.Free.chooseBasis ℤ L`, the basis of the free $\mathbb{Z}$-module `L.carrier` that Lean picks, and applies `Module.Basis.extendOfIsLattice`: since the carrier is a full lattice in $V$, the same vectors form a $\mathbb{Q}$-basis of $V$.

This is the standard fact that a full lattice $L$ in a rational vector space $V$ satisfies $V = \mathbb{Q} \otimes L$, so any $\mathbb{Z}$-basis of $L$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-basis of $V$: denominators can be cleared in a rational relation, and fullness gives spanning.

## What it says
The rational basis of an integral lattice consists of the very vectors of the lattice's chosen integral basis: its $i$-th vector is the $i$-th vector of the $\mathbb{Z}$-basis, seen in the ambient space.

- `[AddCommGroup V] [Module ℚ V]`: $V$ is a vector space over the rationals $\mathbb{Q}$ (an additive commutative group with a $\mathbb{Q}$-module structure); $V$ is any type.
- `(L : IntegralLattice V)`: an integral lattice $L$ in $V$: a full lattice `L.carrier` in $V$ with a symmetric rational bilinear form on $V$ that is integral on it.
- `(i : Module.Free.ChooseBasisIndex ℤ ↥L.carrier)`: an index $i$ of the basis of the carrier that Lean chooses.
- The conclusion: `L.rationalBasis i = ↑((Module.Free.chooseBasis ℤ ↥L.carrier) i)`. The $i$-th vector of `L.rationalBasis`, the $\mathbb{Q}$-basis of $V$, equals the $i$-th vector of the chosen $\mathbb{Z}$-basis of the carrier, carried into $V$ by the inclusion.

This is what makes `rationalBasis` the standard passage from a lattice to its rational span: a $\mathbb{Z}$-basis $e_1, \dots, e_n$ of a full lattice $L$ in $V$ is, as it stands, a $\mathbb{Q}$-basis of $V$, and nothing is changed or added.

## What it says
Multiplying an integral lattice $L$ by an integer $n$ multiplies its bilinear form by $n$: the form of $n \cdot L$ is $n B$, where $B$ is the form of $L$.

- `[AddCommGroup V] [Module ℚ V]`: $V$ is a vector space over the rationals $\mathbb{Q}$ (an additive commutative group with a $\mathbb{Q}$-module structure); $V$ is any type.
- `(n : ℤ)`: an integer $n$, the scaling factor.
- `(L : IntegralLattice V)`: an integral lattice $L$ in $V$: a full lattice in $V$ with a symmetric rational bilinear form `L.form` on $V$ that is integral on it.
- The conclusion: `(n • L).form = ↑n • L.form`. Here `n • L` is $L$ acted on by the integer $n$, through the action of $\mathbb{Z}$ on integral lattices; its form, a bilinear form on all of $V$, is the form of $L$ multiplied by $n$, read as a rational number: $(x, y) \mapsto n\,B(x, y)$.

This is the standard twist $L(n)$ of a lattice, in which the form, and not the lattice vectors, is multiplied by $n$; the lemma records what the action does to the form, for every integer $n$.

## What it says
An integral overlattice $N$ of an integral lattice $L$, with the same form, lies between $L$ and its dual. Viewed as such an intermediate subgroup and made back into an integral lattice, it is $N$ again.

- `[AddCommGroup V] [Module ℚ V]`: $V$ is a vector space over the rationals $\mathbb{Q}$ (an additive commutative group with a $\mathbb{Q}$-module structure); $V$ is any type.
- `(N : IntegralLattice V)`: an integral lattice $N$ in $V$: a full lattice in $V$ with a symmetric rational bilinear form on $V$ that is integral on it.
- `(hform : N.form = L.form)`: the hypothesis `hform` that $N$ has the same form on $V$ as a second integral lattice $L$, an implicit argument read off from it.
- `(hle : L.carrier ≤ N.carrier)`: the hypothesis `hle` that the lattice of $L$ is contained in that of $N$, so $N$ is an overlattice of $L$.
- `[Submodule.IsLattice ℚ ↑(N.toIntermediateCarrier hform hle)]`: the subgroup underlying `N.toIntermediateCarrier hform hle`, which is the carrier of $N$ seen as a subgroup between $L$ and its dual $L^\vee$, is a full lattice in $V$, finitely generated and spanning $V$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.
- `(h : IntermediateCarrier.IsIntegral (N.toIntermediateCarrier hform hle))`: the proof `h` that this intermediate subgroup is integral, lying in its own dual for the form of $L$.
- The conclusion: `h.toIntegralLattice = N`. The integral lattice made from the integral intermediate subgroup, with the form of $L$, is $N$.

This is one half of the standard correspondence between the overlattices of $L$ in the same rational space and the integral subgroups $M$ with $L \subseteq M \subseteq L^\vee$: going from an overlattice to its subgroup and back is the identity.

## What it says
Given an integral lattice $N$ in a rational vector space $V$ that has the same form as an integral lattice $L$ and contains it, this packages $N$ as a module lying between $L$ and its dual $L^\vee$.

- `[AddCommGroup V] [Module ℚ V]`: $V$ is a vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$.
- `(N : IntegralLattice V)`: an integral symmetric lattice in $V$: a $\mathbb{Z}$-submodule `N.carrier` of $V$ with a bilinear form `N.form` on $V$ that takes integer values on it.
- `(hform : N.form = L.form)`: $N$ and a second integral lattice $L$ of $V$ (an implicit argument) carry the same form $b$.
- `(hle : L.carrier ≤ N.carrier)`: $L \subseteq N$, so $N$ is an overlattice of $L$.
- The result, of type `↑L.IntermediateCarrier`: a $\mathbb{Z}$-submodule $M$ of $V$ with $L \subseteq M \subseteq L^\vee$, together with the proof of the two inclusions. Here the dual carrier $L^\vee$ is the set of $x \in V$ with $b(x, y) \in \mathbb{Z}$ for every $y \in L$.

The value is $M = N$, that is `N.carrier`. The first inclusion is `hle`; the second holds because for $x \in N$ and $y \in L$ also $y \in N$, so $b(x, y) \in \mathbb{Z}$ by the integrality of $N$.

This is the chain $L \subseteq N \subseteq L^\vee$ that every integral overlattice satisfies, the chain used in Nikulin §1.4. No nondegeneracy of the form is needed, and none is assumed.

## What it says
The isometry group of the $E_8$ lattice is isomorphic, as a group, to the automorphism group of Tau Ceti's pinned $E_8$ root datum. The declaration has no arguments: it is one specific isomorphism.

- The left side, `typeE₈RootLattice.Isometry typeE₈RootLattice`, is the group $O(E_8)$ of isometries of `typeE₈RootLattice`, the $E_8$ root lattice: the lattice $\mathbb{Z}^8$ in $\mathbb{Q}^8$ (`Fin 8 → ℚ`) whose Gram matrix in the standard basis, the simple roots, is the $E_8$ Cartan matrix. An isometry is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear bijection of $\mathbb{Q}^8$ that preserves the form and maps the lattice onto itself.
- The right side, `RootPairing.Aut DynkinType.e8SimplyConnectedRootDatum`, is the automorphism group of the pinned simply connected root datum of type $E_8$, with 240 roots and weight and coweight lattices $\mathbb{Z}^8$ (`Fin 8 → ℤ`): the $\mathbb{Z}$-linear automorphisms of the weight lattice that permute the roots, with the matching action on the coroots.
- `≃*`: a bijection that respects the group laws.

The value is `MulEquiv.ofBijective` applied to a homomorphism `typeE₈IsometryToAutHom` from isometries to automorphisms, with proofs that it is injective and surjective. As the docstring says, an isometry acts on the weight lattice through the identification of the lattice with the weight lattice that sends $x$ to its eight inner products with the simple roots; this is a bijection since the $E_8$ Cartan matrix has determinant $1$.

This is the classical fact that the automorphisms of the $E_8$ lattice are the automorphisms of its root system, the 240 vectors of norm $2$. Since $E_8$ is unimodular, its root lattice is its weight lattice, so nothing is lost in passing to the datum.

- `RootPairing.Aut` is the group of all automorphisms of the datum, not only those that fix its pinning, the chosen simple roots: those alone form the trivial group, as the $E_8$ Dynkin diagram has no symmetries.
- "Simply connected" makes the datum's weight lattice the full weight lattice; for $E_8$ it equals the root lattice.
- The definition is `noncomputable`: the inverse map comes from bijectivity by classical choice, but an inverse is unique, so nothing arbitrary is chosen.

## What it says
The group isomorphism `typeE₈IsometryEquivAut`, from the isometry group of the $E_8$ lattice to the automorphism group of the pinned $E_8$ root datum, sends the reflection in the $i$-th root of the lattice to the reflection of the datum in its $i$-th root.

- `(i : Fin 240)`: an index $i$ of one of the 240 roots, $0 \le i < 240$.
- The conclusion: `typeE₈RootVector i` is the $i$-th root $\alpha_i$ of the $E_8$ lattice, a lattice vector with $(\alpha_i, \alpha_i) = 2$, and `rootReflection (typeE₈RootVector i) ⋯` is the reflection $x \mapsto x - (x, \alpha_i)\,\alpha_i$, an isometry of the lattice. Its image under `typeE₈IsometryEquivAut` equals `RootPairing.Equiv.reflection DynkinType.e8SimplyConnectedRootDatum i`, the automorphism of the datum given by the reflection in its $i$-th root: $\lambda \mapsto \lambda - \langle \lambda, \alpha_i^\vee \rangle\, \alpha_i$ on weights, with the matching action on coweights and on the indices of the roots.

This is the compatibility one expects. The isomorphism identifies the lattice with the datum's weight lattice by pairing with the simple roots; under it, pairing with a lattice root becomes pairing with the corresponding coroot, since $E_8$ is simply laced. As a reflection determines its root up to sign, the lemma also says that this identification takes the $i$-th root of the lattice to $\pm$ the $i$-th root of the datum: the two numberings of the roots agree.

## What it says
For an isometry $g$ of the $E_8$ lattice, the automorphism of the pinned $E_8$ root datum that `typeE₈IsometryEquivAut` attaches to $g$ permutes the indices of the 240 roots exactly as $g$ permutes the roots of the lattice.

- `(i : Fin 240)`: an index $i$ of one of the 240 roots.
- The conclusion: let $\sigma$ be `(↑(typeE₈IsometryEquivAut g)).indexEquiv`, the permutation of the root indices $\{0, \dots, 239\}$ that comes with the datum automorphism attached to $g$. Then `typeE₈RootVector` at $\sigma(i)$, the lattice root with index $\sigma(i)$, equals `g.carrierEquiv (typeE₈RootVector i)`, the image under $g$ of the lattice root $\alpha_i$ with index $i$. In short, $\alpha_{\sigma(i)} = g(\alpha_i)$.

As the docstring says, this characterizes the isomorphism: an automorphism of a root system is determined by its permutation of the roots, since the roots span, and the lemma gives that permutation in terms of $g$. It is the compatibility one expects: the datum automorphism moves the roots as $g$ does.

## What it says
In the discriminant group of the rank-one lattice $\langle a \rangle$, the $k$-th multiple of the distinguished class $g = 1/a + \mathbb{Z}$ is the class of $k/a$.

- `(a : ℤ)`: an integer $a$; the lattice `rankOne a` is $\langle a \rangle$, the integers $\mathbb{Z}$ inside $\mathbb{Q}$ with the form $B(x, y) = a\,x y$. Its dual carrier, the $x \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $B(x, y) \in \mathbb{Z}$ for every $y \in \mathbb{Z}$, is $\frac{1}{a}\mathbb{Z}$, and its discriminant group is $\frac{1}{a}\mathbb{Z} / \mathbb{Z}$.
- `[NeZero a]`: the hypothesis $a \neq 0$.
- `(k : ℤ)`: an integer $k$.
- The conclusion: `k • rankOneClass a`, $k$ times the distinguished class $g = 1/a + \mathbb{Z}$ in the discriminant group, equals `Submodule.Quotient.mk (k • rankOneDualGen a)`, the class modulo $\mathbb{Z}$ of $k$ times the dual vector $1/a$, that is $k/a + \mathbb{Z}$.

The discriminant group of $\langle a \rangle$ is cyclic of order $|a|$, generated by $1/a + \mathbb{Z}$; the lemma records that $k g$ is represented by $k/a$, as it is since passing to classes is additive.

## What it says
The volume of the orthogonal group $O(n)$ is $\prod_{j=1}^{n} 2\pi^{j/2}/\Gamma(j/2)$, the product of the areas of the unit spheres $S^0, S^1, \dots, S^{n-1}$.

- `(n : ℕ)`: a natural number $n$, the size of the matrices; $n = 0$ is allowed.
- The conclusion: `orthogonalGroupVolume n`, the volume of $O(n)$ for the measure `orthogonalGroupMeasure` that Tau Ceti puts on it, equals the product over $j$ in $\{1, \dots, n\}$ (`Finset.Icc 1 n`) of $2\pi^{j/2}/\Gamma(j/2)$, which is the area of the unit sphere $S^{j-1}$ in $\mathbb{R}^j$.

As the docstring says, the formula comes from the tower of fibrations $O(j) \to S^{j-1}$ with fibre $O(j-1)$: each step multiplies the volume by the area of a sphere. This is the standard value of $\operatorname{vol} O(n)$ in that normalisation, the one used in the mass formula for lattices: $\operatorname{vol} O(1) = 2$, $\operatorname{vol} O(2) = 4\pi$, $\operatorname{vol} O(3) = 16\pi^2$.

## Lean subtleties
- `Finset.Icc 1 n` is the finite set $\{1, \dots, n\}$. For $n = 0$ it is empty and the product is $1$, the volume of $O(0)$, a single point.
- `↑j / 2` is the natural number $j$ cast to a real number and then halved: $j/2$ is a half-integer, not rounded down as division of natural numbers would be. `Real.pi ^ (↑j / 2)` is the real power $\pi^{j/2}$.
- `Real.Gamma` is Euler's Gamma function. It is evaluated here only at the positive numbers $j/2$, where it takes its classical values, so no junk value enters.
- The value depends on how the measure on $O(n)$ is normalised. In the normalisation here, each fibration $O(j) \to S^{j-1}$ multiplies the volume by exactly the area of $S^{j-1}$, and $O(1) = \{\pm 1\}$ has volume $2$. The metric that $n \times n$ matrices inherit from $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ would give $2^{n(n-1)/4}$ times this.

## What it says
For a flat module $M$ over a commutative semiring $R$, and an $R$-algebra $K$ into which $R$ embeds, the canonical isomorphism of $M$ with the unit pure tensors $1 \otimes m$ of $K \otimes_R M$ sends $m$ to $1 \otimes m$.

- `[CommSemiring R]`: $R$ is a commutative semiring, a commutative ring in which subtraction may be missing.
- `[Semiring K] [Algebra R K]`: $K$ is an $R$-algebra: a semiring with a structure map from $R$ into its centre.
- `[AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M]`: $M$ is an $R$-module.
- `[FaithfulSMul R K]`: $R$ acts faithfully on $K$; for an algebra this says that the structure map $R \to K$ is injective.
- `[Module.Flat R M]`: $M$ is flat over $R$.
- `(m : M)`: an element $m$ of $M$.
- The conclusion: `unitTmulEquiv R K M` is the $R$-linear isomorphism of $M$ with the submodule `((mk R K M) 1).range` of $K \otimes_R M$, the image of the map $m \mapsto 1 \otimes m$. Its value at $m$, viewed through the arrow `↑` as an element of $K \otimes_R M$, is the pure tensor `1 ⊗ₜ[R] m`, that is $1 \otimes m$.

The isomorphism exists because $m \mapsto 1 \otimes m$ is injective: it is $M \cong R \otimes_R M \to K \otimes_R M$, the injection $R \to K$ tensored with the flat module $M$. The lemma says that the isomorphism is this map; as the docstring says, the equation characterizes it.

- `(hγab : γ a = γ b)`: the curve is closed.

## What it says
The isoperimetric inequality for closed plane curves traversed at constant speed: $4\pi|A| \le L^2$, where $L$ is the length of the curve and $A$ its signed area.

- `(hγ : HasConstantSpeedOnWith γ (Set.Icc a b) l)`: the curve $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$, a plane curve with $\mathbb{C}$ as the plane, has constant speed $l \ge 0$ on $[a, b]$: for $a \le x \le y \le b$, the length of $\gamma$ on $[x, y]$ is $l(y - x)$.
- `(hab : a ≤ b)`: $[a, b]$ is an interval, possibly a single point.
- `(hγab : γ a = γ b)`: the curve is closed.
- The conclusion: $4\pi\,|A| \le L^2$, where $A$ is `TauCeti.signedArea γ a b`, the signed area $\frac12 \int_a^b (x y' - y x')\,dt$ for $\gamma = x + iy$, and $L$ is `(eVariationOn γ (Set.Icc a b)).toReal`, the total variation of $\gamma$ on $[a, b]$, which is its length.

This is the classical isoperimetric inequality $L^2 \ge 4\pi|A|$, for curves parametrised proportionally to arc length, arclength parametrisations among them. For a simple closed curve $|A|$ is the enclosed area; for other closed curves it is the area counted with winding number. At constant speed $(b - a)\int_a^b |\gamma'|^2 = L^2$, so the inequality is the area–energy inequality $4\pi|A| \le (b-a)\int_a^b |\gamma'|^2$ in another form.

This is the inequality at the heart of Hurwitz's Fourier proof of the isoperimetric inequality. With $c_n$ the Fourier coefficients of $\gamma$ on $[a, b]$, the right side is $4\pi^2 \sum n^2 |c_n|^2$ and the left is $4\pi^2 \left|\sum n |c_n|^2\right|$, and $n^2 \ge |n|$ for integers. - `(hL2 : MeasureTheory.MemLp γ' 2 (MeasureTheory.volume.restrict (Set.Ioc a b)))`: $\gamma'$ is square-integrable on $(a, b]$.

This is the classical computation: $x y' - y x'$ is the imaginary part of $\bar\gamma \gamma'$; since the curve is closed, the coefficients of $\gamma'$ are $2\pi i n/(b-a)$ times those of $\gamma$, and Parseval's identity turns the integral into the sum. ## What it says
Cartan's criterion. Let $B$ be a set of quasi-compact open subsets of a space $X$, closed under binary intersections and containing, inside each of its members, a basis of the topology of that member. A sheaf of abelian groups $F$ that is Čech acyclic for finite covers of members of $B$ by members of $B$ has no cohomology in positive degrees on the members of $B$.

Here $X$ is a topological space, $B$ a set of its open subsets, $F$ a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$ and $Y$ an open subset, all implicit.

- `(hinf : ∀ U ∈ B, ∀ V ∈ B, U ⊓ V ∈ B)`: $B$ is closed under intersections of two members.
- `(hcpt : ∀ U ∈ B, IsCompact ↑U)`: every member of $B$ is quasi-compact.
- `(hbasis : ∀ U ∈ B, ∀ V ≤ U, ∀ x ∈ V, ∃ W ∈ B, x ∈ W ∧ W ≤ V)`: for $U \in B$, every open $V \subseteq U$ and every $x \in V$, some $W \in B$ has $x \in W \subseteq V$; so the members of $B$ inside $U$ form a basis of $U$.
- `(hF : IsCechAcyclicOn B F)`: for every $Y' \in B$ and every finite nonempty family of members of $B$ covering $Y'$, the augmented Čech complex of $F$ for the induced cover of $Y'$ is exact.
- `(hY : Y ∈ B)`: $Y$ is a member of $B$.
- `(n : ℕ)`: a natural number $n$; the degree is $n + 1 \ge 1$.
- The conclusion: the sheaf cohomology group $H^{n+1}(Y, F)$ has at most one element, so it is zero.

Cartan's criterion in the literature allows any basis and any cofinal system of covers. This is the special case where the members of $B$ are quasi-compact and the covers are finite: every open cover of a member of $B$ is then refined by a finite cover by members of $B$, so these covers are cofinal.

## What it says
Purity of the branch locus over a two-dimensional regular local ring: a finite, torsion-free algebra $B$ over such a ring $A$, whose localizations at maximal ideals are normal domains, is étale over $A$ as soon as it is unramified at every prime not lying over the closed point.

- `[CommRing A] [CommRing B] [Algebra A B]`: $A$ and $B$ are commutative rings and $B$ is an $A$-algebra.
- `[IsRegularLocalRing A]`: $A$ is a regular local ring: Noetherian, local, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ generated by $\dim A$ elements.
- `[Module.Finite A B] [Module.IsTorsionFree A B]`: $B$ is finitely generated as an $A$-module and torsion-free: a nonzero $a \in A$ kills no nonzero element of $B$.
- `(hdim : ringKrullDim A = 2)`: $A$ has Krull dimension $2$.
- `(hnormal : ∀ (𝔮 : Ideal B) [inst : 𝔮.IsMaximal], IsDomain (Localization.AtPrime 𝔮) ∧ IsIntegrallyClosed (Localization.AtPrime 𝔮))`: for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak{q}$ of $B$, the local ring $B_{\mathfrak{q}}$ is a domain, integrally closed in its fraction field.
- `(hunram : ∀ (q : Ideal B) [inst : q.IsPrime], Ideal.under A q ≠ IsLocalRing.maximalIdeal A → Algebra.IsUnramifiedAt A q)`: for every prime $q$ of $B$ with $q \cap A \neq \mathfrak{m}$, $B$ is unramified over $A$ at $q$.
- The conclusion: `Algebra.Etale A B`, $B$ is étale over $A$.

In geometric terms, a finite normal cover of $\operatorname{Spec} A$ that is étale over the punctured spectrum is étale everywhere, the dimension-two case of purity. Torsion-freeness keeps out components supported on the closed point: $A \times A/\mathfrak{m}$ satisfies every other hypothesis but is not flat over $A$.

## What it says
This is Galois descent for an étale algebra. Let $A$ be an étale algebra over a field $K$, and $\Omega$ a separable closure of $K$. A function $h$ from the $\Omega$-valued points of $A$ to $\Omega$ is evaluation at an element of $A$ if and only if it is $\mathrm{Gal}(\Omega/K)$-equivariant.

- `[Field K] [Field Ω] [Algebra K Ω]`: $K$ and $\Omega$ are fields, and $\Omega$ is an extension of $K$.
- `[CommRing A] [Algebra K A]`: $A$ is a commutative $K$-algebra.
- `[IsSepClosed Ω] [IsGalois K Ω]`: $\Omega$ is separably closed and Galois (separable and normal) over $K$. Together these say that $\Omega$ is a separable closure of $K$.
- `[Etale K A]`: $A$ is étale over $K$, meaning formally étale and of finite presentation. Over a field these are the finite products of finite separable extensions of $K$.
- `(h : (A →ₐ[K] Ω) → Ω)`: a function $h$ that assigns an element of $\Omega$ to each $K$-algebra map $\varphi\colon A \to \Omega$ (each point of $A$).
- The conclusion has two sides. On the left, $h$ lies in the range of `AlgHom.pi fun (φ : A →ₐ[K] Ω) => φ`, the $K$-algebra map from $A$ to all functions from points to $\Omega$ that sends $a$ to $(\varphi \mapsto \varphi(a))$. That is, $h(\varphi) = \varphi(a)$ for some $a \in A$ and all $\varphi$. On the right, $h(\sigma \circ \varphi) = \sigma(h(\varphi))$ for every $\sigma \in \mathrm{Gal}(\Omega/K)$ and every point $\varphi$. The statement is that the two are equivalent.

This is the classical descent statement. For étale $A$, $\Omega \otimes_K A$ is the algebra of all functions from points to $\Omega$. Under that identification, the invariants of the Galois action on the factor $\Omega$ are the equivariant functions on one side, and $A$ on the other, since the fixed field of $\mathrm{Gal}(\Omega/K)$ is $K$.

## What it says
Let $A$ be an étale algebra over a field $K$, and $\Omega$ a separably closed field containing $K$. Then the $\Omega$-valued points of $A$ separate its elements: if $\varphi(a) = \varphi(b)$ for every $K$-algebra map $\varphi\colon A \to \Omega$, then $a = b$.

- `[CommRing A] [Algebra K A]`: $A$ is a commutative $K$-algebra.
- `[IsSepClosed Ω]`: $\Omega$ is separably closed: every separable polynomial over $\Omega$ splits in $\Omega$. Nothing asks $\Omega$ to be algebraic over $K$.
- `[Etale K A]`: $A$ is étale over $K$, meaning formally étale and of finite presentation. Over a field these are the finite products of finite separable extensions of $K$.
- The conclusion: `AlgHom.pi fun (φ : A →ₐ[K] Ω) => φ` is injective. This is the $K$-algebra map from $A$ to the algebra of $\Omega$-valued functions on the set of points, $a \mapsto (\varphi \mapsto \varphi(a))$.

This is the standard fact behind Galois theory for étale algebras. Each factor of $A$, a finite separable extension of $K$, embeds into the separably closed $\Omega$, and a field map is injective. The hypothesis on $\Omega$ cannot simply be dropped. For $\Omega = K$ and $A$ a separable quadratic extension of $K$ there are no points at all, and the map to the zero algebra is not injective.

## What it says
Affine morphisms satisfy fpqc descent. A morphism of schemes whose base change along a surjective, flat and quasi-compact morphism is affine is itself affine.

The declaration takes no arguments. It is an instance, which provides `DescendsAlong (@IsAffineHom) (@Surjective ⊓ @Flat ⊓ @QuasiCompact)` in the category of schemes. It says: take a pullback square of schemes with $f\colon X \to Z$ surjective, flat and quasi-compact, and any $g\colon Y \to Z$. If the base change $X \times_Z Y \to X$ of $g$ along $f$ is affine, then $g$ is affine.

- `IsAffineHom`: a morphism is affine when the preimage of every affine open subset of the target is affine.
- `Surjective ⊓ Flat ⊓ QuasiCompact`: the morphisms that are surjective (on underlying spaces), flat, and quasi-compact (preimages of quasi-compact opens are quasi-compact). These are the faithfully flat quasi-compact morphisms, the coverings of fpqc descent.

This is the descent half of the classical statement that being affine is local on the base for the fpqc topology. The other half, that affine morphisms are stable under base change, is not part of this declaration. It is stated for a single surjective, flat, quasi-compact morphism rather than for a covering family. Since being affine is Zariski-local on the base, the single-morphism form gives the usual one.

Every finite continuous Galois set is the set of points of a finite étale algebra. For a Galois extension $\Omega/K$, the functor `galoisFiber K Ω` is essentially surjective. That functor sends a finite étale $K$-algebra $A$ to the finite set $\mathrm{Hom}_K(A, \Omega)$ with its action of $\mathrm{Gal}(\Omega/K)$.

This is the essential-surjectivity half of Galois theory for étale algebras over a field. For $\Omega$ a separable closure, $A \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}_K(A, \Omega)$ is an anti-equivalence between finite étale $K$-algebras and finite continuous $\mathrm{Gal}(\Omega/K)$-sets. Essential surjectivity needs only that $\Omega$ be Galois. A transitive continuous Galois set is $\mathrm{Gal}(\Omega/K)/\mathrm{Gal}(\Omega/M) \cong \mathrm{Hom}_K(M, \Omega)$ for a finite extension $M \subseteq \Omega$ of $K$, and finite sets are disjoint unions of orbits, which come from products of algebras.

The fibre functor at a separably closed field is faithful. Two maps of finite étale $K$-algebras that induce the same map on $\Omega$-valued points are equal.

This functor is faithful: if $\psi \circ f = \psi \circ g$ for every point $\psi$ of $B$, then $f = g$.

This is the faithfulness part of Galois theory for étale algebras. It holds because the $\Omega$-points of the finite étale algebra $B$ separate its elements, so $\psi(f(a)) = \psi(g(a))$ for all $\psi$ forces $f(a) = g(a)$. Separable closedness cannot be dropped. Over $\Omega = K$, a separable quadratic extension $L$ of $K$ has no points, so the identity of $L$ and its conjugation induce the same (empty) map, yet they differ.

For general $\Omega$ the same functor is defined, with no claim beyond that.

## What it says
This is the functor sending a finite étale $K$-algebra $A$ to the finite $\mathrm{Gal}(\Omega/K)$-set $\mathrm{Hom}_K(A, \Omega)$ of its $\Omega$-valued points, with the Galois group acting by postcomposition. No continuity is recorded here.

- `[Field K] [Field Ω] [Algebra K Ω]`: $K$ and $\Omega$ are fields, and $\Omega$ is an extension of $K$. It need not be Galois over $K$ or separably closed.
- The type, `CategoryTheory.Functor (CommAlgCat.FiniteEtale K)ᵒᵖ (Action FintypeCat Gal(Ω/K))`: a functor from the opposite of the category of finite étale $K$-algebras to the category of finite sets with an action of $\mathrm{Gal}(\Omega/K)$.

Its value has two parts.
- On objects: $A$ goes to the finite set $\mathrm{Hom}_K(A, \Omega)$, the value at $A$ of the fibre functor `CommAlgCat.FiniteEtale.fiber K Ω`. On it, $\sigma \in \mathrm{Gal}(\Omega/K)$ acts by $\sigma \cdot \varphi = \sigma \circ \varphi$, and the two are bundled into a $G$-set by `Action.FintypeCat.ofMulAction`.
- On morphisms: a $K$-algebra map $f\colon A \to B$ goes to the fibre functor's map, precomposition $\psi \mapsto \psi \circ f$, from $\mathrm{Hom}_K(B, \Omega)$ to $\mathrm{Hom}_K(A, \Omega)$. It is equivariant because $(\sigma \circ \psi) \circ f = \sigma \circ (\psi \circ f)$.

This is the standard Galois-set structure on the points of an étale algebra, the one the fundamental theorem of Galois theory for étale algebras is about. Adding continuity of the action gives `galoisFiber`, as the docstring says.

## What it says
For a separable closure $\Omega$ of a field $K$, the functor `galoisFiber K Ω`, which sends a finite étale $K$-algebra $A$ to the finite set $\mathrm{Hom}_K(A, \Omega)$ of its $\Omega$-valued points with its continuous action of $\mathrm{Gal}(\Omega/K)$, is fully faithful: for finite étale $A$ and $B$, the $K$-algebra maps $A \to B$ correspond bijectively, by precomposition, to the $\mathrm{Gal}(\Omega/K)$-equivariant maps $\mathrm{Hom}_K(B,\Omega) \to \mathrm{Hom}_K(A,\Omega)$.

- `[Field K] [Field Ω] [Algebra K Ω]`: `K` and `Ω` are fields, types in one universe `u`, and `Ω` is a field extension of `K`.
- `[IsSepClosed Ω]`: `Ω` is separably closed.
- `[IsGalois K Ω]`: the extension $\Omega/K$ is Galois: normal and separable, so algebraic. With the previous hypothesis, `Ω` is a separable closure of `K`.
- The value: a `FullyFaithful` structure for `galoisFiber K Ω`, the functor from the opposite of the category of finite étale `K`-algebras to `ContAction FintypeCat Gal(Ω/K)`, the finite sets with a continuous action of the Galois group. It holds the inverse of the map the functor induces on morphisms, with the two laws that make it an inverse, and is built (`.ofFullyFaithful`) from the facts that the functor is full and faithful.

This is the full-faithfulness half of Galois theory for finite étale algebras over a field, which makes them anti-equivalent to finite continuous Galois sets; it is stated, as there, for a separable closure.

## What it says
For any field extension $\Omega$ of $K$ and any finite étale $K$-algebra $A$, the action of $\mathrm{Gal}(\Omega/K)$ by postcomposition on the finite set $\mathrm{Hom}_K(A,\Omega)$ of $\Omega$-valued points of $A$ is continuous, for the topology of the Galois group and the discrete topology on the finite set.

- `[Field K] [Field Ω] [Algebra K Ω]`: `K` and `Ω` are fields, types in one universe `u`, and `Ω` is a `K`-algebra, so a field extension of `K`.
- `(A : (CommAlgCat.FiniteEtale K)ᵒᵖ)`: an object $A$ of the opposite of the category of finite étale `K`-algebras, that is, a finite étale `K`-algebra, taken in the opposite category because points are contravariant in $A$.
- The conclusion: `(galoisFiberAction K Ω).obj A` is the finite set $\mathrm{Hom}_K(A,\Omega)$ with $\mathrm{Gal}(\Omega/K)$ acting by $\varphi \mapsto \sigma \circ \varphi$, an object of `Action FintypeCat Gal(Ω/K)`. It has the property `Action.isContinuous`: the action map $\mathrm{Gal}(\Omega/K) \times \mathrm{Hom}_K(A,\Omega) \to \mathrm{Hom}_K(A,\Omega)$ is continuous when the finite set carries its discrete topology, which amounts to each point having an open stabilizer.

This is the standard fact that the Galois sets coming from étale algebras are continuous: a point $\varphi$ is fixed by every automorphism fixing $\varphi(A)$, a finite extension of $K$, and those form an open subgroup. As the docstring says, the group then acts trivially on the intersection of the finitely many stabilizers, an open subgroup. It is the property that `ContAction` asks of an object of `Action`.

## What it says
For a tower of scalars $R \to A \to B$ and an $R$-module $M$, two ways of tensoring the map $A \to B$ with $M$ give the same function $A \otimes_R M \to B \otimes_R M$: the $A$-linear one built from the structure map of $B$ as an $A$-algebra, and the $R$-linear one built from that map seen as an $R$-algebra homomorphism. Both send $a \otimes m$ to $(a \cdot 1_B) \otimes m$.

- `[CommSemiring R] [CommSemiring A] [Semiring B]`: $R$ and $A$ are commutative semirings and $B$ is a semiring, not necessarily commutative; rings are the main case.
- `[Algebra R A] [Algebra R B] [Algebra A B]`: $A$ and $B$ are $R$-algebras, and $B$ is an $A$-algebra.
- `[IsScalarTower R A B]`: the three are compatible, $(r a) b = r (a b)$, so the map $R \to B$ is the composite $R \to A \to B$.
- `[AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M]`: $M$ is an $R$-module (an additive commutative monoid with scalars from $R$).
- `(x : TensorProduct R A M)`: an element x of $A \otimes_R M$.
- The conclusion: `((rTensor R M) (Algebra.linearMap A B)) x`, the image of x under the $A$-linear map $A \otimes_R M \to B \otimes_R M$ that `AlgebraTensorModule.rTensor` makes from the $A$-linear structure map $a \mapsto a \cdot 1_B$, equals `(LinearMap.rTensor M (IsScalarTower.toAlgHom R A B).toLinearMap) x`, its image under $f \otimes \mathrm{id}_M$, for $f : A \to B$ the same map as an $R$-algebra homomorphism.

Both sides are $f \otimes \mathrm{id}_M$ for one and the same function $f$, and differ only in the linearity they carry, so this is the expected identification of the two base changes.

## What it says
For a commutative ring $R$ and a Weierstrass curve $W$ over $R$ whose discriminant is a unit, this is the elliptic curve over $\mathrm{Spec}\,R$ that $W$ defines: the projective cubic of $W$, with its projection to $\mathrm{Spec}\,R$ and the point $[0:1:0]$ as zero section.

- `[CommRing R]`: R is a commutative ring with $1$, any one, on a type in a universe `u`.
- `(W : WeierstrassCurve R)`: a Weierstrass curve W over R, given by coefficients $a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4, a_6 \in R$, standing for $Y^2 + a_1XY + a_3Y = X^3 + a_2X^2 + a_4X + a_6$.
- `[W.IsElliptic]`: the discriminant $\Delta$ of W is a unit of $R$.
- The value, an `EllipticCurveGeom` over `Spec ↧R`: its total space is the projective Weierstrass model, the cubic $Y^2Z + a_1XYZ + a_3YZ^2 = X^3 + a_2X^2Z + a_4XZ^2 + a_6Z^3$ over $R$ built as a $\mathrm{Proj}$; its structure morphism is the projection of that model to $\mathrm{Spec}\,R$; its zero section is the point $[0:1:0]$. Smoothness of relative dimension one and properness are results found by instance search. Its local model, a pointed Weierstrass atlas, has a single chart over the whole base, whose equation is W itself and whose comparison with the projective model is the identity.

This is the standard way a Weierstrass equation with invertible discriminant gives an elliptic curve over $\mathrm{Spec}\,R$: the smooth proper projective cubic, pointed by its point at infinity. It builds a curve from one global equation; it does not say that every elliptic curve over $\mathrm{Spec}\,R$ has one.

## What it says
For a cusp form f of weight $k$ for a group $\mathcal{G}$, this is the conjugate cusp form $f^\rho(\tau) = \overline{f(-\overline{\tau})}$, a cusp form of the same weight for any group $\mathcal{G}'$ inside the conjugate of $\mathcal{G}$ by $J = \mathrm{diag}(-1, 1)$.

- `(f : CuspForm 𝒢 k)`: f is a cusp form of weight $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ (implicit) for `𝒢`: a holomorphic function on the upper half-plane, invariant under the weight-$k$ slash action of `𝒢`, and zero at infinity at the cusps.

This is the standard conjugate, or dual, form: if $f = \sum a_n q^n$ then $f^\rho = \sum \overline{a_n}\, q^n$, since $e^{2\pi i n(-\overline{\tau})} = \overline{e^{2\pi i n \tau}}$. ## What it says
The completed L-function of a cusp form at level $N$: the Mellin transform $\int_0^\infty f(it/\sqrt{N})\, t^{s-1}\, dt$.

- `(N : ℕ+)`: a positive integer N, the level.
- `(s : ℂ)`: the complex variable s.
- The value: `mellin` of $t \mapsto f(it/\sqrt{N})$ at s, that is $\int_0^\infty t^{s-1} f(it/\sqrt{N})\, dt$, the integral of f along the imaginary axis rescaled by $1/\sqrt{N}$.

Substituting $t = \sqrt{N}\,y$ turns it into $N^{s/2}\int_0^\infty y^{s-1} f(iy)\, dy$, and for $f = \sum_{n \ge 1} a_n q^n$ the integral term by term gives $N^{s/2}(2\pi)^{-s}\Gamma(s)L(f,s)$. This is the classical completed L-function $\Lambda(f,s)$ of a form of level $N$, the one in the functional equation $s \leftrightarrow k - s$ under the Fricke involution.

## What it says
The analytic conductor of a newform f of level $N$ and weight $k$: its analytic conductor at the central point $s = k/2$, which works out to $N(|k/2| + 3)(|k/2 + 1| + 3)$, that is $N(k/2 + 3)(k/2 + 4)$ in positive weight.

- `[NeZero N]`: the level $N$, a natural number (implicit), is not $0$.
- `(f : Newform N k)`: a newform f of level $N$ and weight $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ (implicit): a Hecke eigenform in the new subspace, normalised by $a_1 = 1$.
- The value: `f.analyticConductorAt ((k : ℂ) / 2)`, the real number that `analyticConductorAt` gives at the arithmetic parameter $s = k/2$, the centre of the functional equation $s \leftrightarrow k - s$.

In the analytic variable $s_{an} = s - (k-1)/2$, the gamma factor of a weight-$k$ newform has the shifts $\kappa_1 = (k-1)/2$ and $\kappa_2 = (k+1)/2$, and the analytic conductor in the sense of Iwaniec and Kowalski is $N\prod_j(|s_{an} + \kappa_j| + 3)$. At the centre, $s_{an} = 1/2$, this is $N(k/2+3)(k/2+4)$, the value the first test gives. Evaluating at the central point is the usual way to attach one number to the form.

## What it says

## What it says
The conjugate, or dual, newform of a newform f of nebentypus χ: the newform $f_\rho(\tau) = \overline{f(-\overline{\tau})}$ of the same level and weight, with nebentypus $\chi^{-1}$, whose Hecke eigenvalues and $q$-expansion coefficients are the complex conjugates of those of f.

- `[NeZero N]`: the level $N$, a natural number (implicit), is not $0$.
- `(f : Newform N k)`: a newform f of level $N$ and weight $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ (implicit): a nonzero Hecke eigenform for $\Gamma_1(N)$ with a nebentypus χ, in the new subspace and normalised by $a_1 = 1$.
- The value, a `Newform N k` with these fields:
  - its cusp form is the conjugate cusp form `CuspForm.conj` of f, $\tau \mapsto \overline{f(-\overline{\tau})}$, again on $\Gamma_1(N)$;
  - its nebentypus is $\chi^{-1}$, and it lies in the space of forms with that character;
  - its Hecke eigenvalues are the complex conjugates $\overline{\lambda_n}$ of those of f;
  - the remaining fields are proofs that this is again a Hecke eigenform with those eigenvalues, nonzero, new, and with $a_1 = 1$.

This is the standard dual form: if $f = \sum a_n q^n$ then $f_\rho = \sum \overline{a_n}\, q^n$. A Dirichlet character takes its values in the roots of unity, so its complex conjugate is $\chi^{-1}$, the character the construction gives.

For a general nebentypus the Fricke involution does not send f to a multiple of itself but to a multiple of $f_\rho$; the factor is the pseudo-eigenvalue of Atkin and Li, a complex number of absolute value $1$. For trivial character $f_\rho = f$, and it is the Fricke eigenvalue, $\pm 1$.

- `(L : PeriodPair)`: a pair of complex numbers $\omega_1, \omega_2$, linearly independent over $\mathbb{R}$, spanning the lattice $\Lambda = \mathbb{Z}\omega_1 + \mathbb{Z}\omega_2$ (`L.lattice`).
- `(l : ↥L.lattice)`: a point $l$ of $\Lambda$, any one.
- The conclusion: `L.quasiPeriod l`, the quasi-period $\eta(l)$, the constant value of $\zeta(z + l) - \zeta(z)$, equals $2\zeta(l/2)$, where `L.weierstrassZeta` is $\zeta(z) = \frac{1}{z} + \sum_{l' \neq 0} \left(\frac{1}{z - l'} + \frac{1}{l'} + \frac{z}{l'^2}\right)$.

When $l/2 \notin \Lambda$ this is the classical identity: $\zeta$ is odd, and quasi-periodicity at $z = -l/2$ gives $\zeta(l/2) = \zeta(-l/2) + \eta(l) = -\zeta(l/2) + \eta(l)$. With $l$ twice a half-period it is the classical formula for the quasi-periods as values of $\zeta$ at the half-periods.

## What it says
The quasi-periodicity of the Weierstrass zeta function: $\zeta(z + l) = \zeta(z) + \eta(l)$ for every $z \in \mathbb{C}$ and every $l \in \Lambda$.

- `(L : PeriodPair)`: a pair of complex numbers $\omega_1, \omega_2$, linearly independent over $\mathbb{R}$, spanning the lattice $\Lambda = \mathbb{Z}\omega_1 + \mathbb{Z}\omega_2$ (`L.lattice`).
- `(z : ℂ)`: a complex number $z$, any one.
- `(l : ↥L.lattice)`: a point $l$ of $\Lambda$.
- The conclusion: `L.weierstrassZeta`, the function $\zeta(z) = \frac{1}{z} + \sum_{l' \neq 0} \left(\frac{1}{z - l'} + \frac{1}{l'} + \frac{z}{l'^2}\right)$, satisfies $\zeta(z + l) = \zeta(z) + \eta(l)$, where `L.quasiPeriod l` is the quasi-period $\eta(l)$.

This is the classical quasi-periodicity of $\zeta$: off $\Lambda$, $\zeta(z + l) - \zeta(z)$ has derivative $\wp(z) - \wp(z + l) = 0$ on the connected set $\mathbb{C} \setminus \Lambda$, so it is a constant, and $\eta(l)$ is defined as that constant. $\zeta$ is not periodic, but it changes by a constant along each period.

## What it says
The terms of the series of the Weierstrass zeta function are $O(|l|^{-3})$, uniformly for $s$ in a disc: if $|s| < r$ and $|l| \ge 2r$, then $\left|\frac{1}{s - l} + \frac{1}{l} + \frac{s}{l^2}\right| \le 2r^2|l|^{-3}$. The real number $r$ and the complex numbers $s, l$ are implicit.

- `(hs : ‖s‖ < r)`: $s$ lies in the open disc of radius $r$ about $0$.
- `(h : 2 * r ≤ ‖l‖)`: $|l| \ge 2r$.
- The conclusion: the term $\frac{1}{s - l} + \frac{1}{l} + \frac{s}{l^2}$, which equals $\frac{s^2}{l^2(s - l)}$, has absolute value at most $2r^2|l|^{-3}$.

This is the standard estimate behind the convergence of the series for $\zeta$: $|s|^2 < r^2$ and $|s - l| \ge |l| - |s| \ge |l|/2$ give the bound, and since $\sum_{l \neq 0} |l|^{-3}$ converges over a lattice, the Weierstrass M-test applies on each disc.

## What it says
The Weierstrass $\zeta$ function of a lattice is odd: $\zeta(-z) = -\zeta(z)$ for every complex number $z$.

- `(L : PeriodPair)`: a period pair, two complex numbers $\omega_1, \omega_2$ that are linearly independent over $\mathbb{R}$. They span the lattice $\Lambda = \mathbb{Z}\omega_1 + \mathbb{Z}\omega_2$ in $\mathbb{C}$.
- `(z : ℂ)`: a complex number, with no condition on it.
- The conclusion: `L.weierstrassZeta (-z) = -L.weierstrassZeta z`, that is $\zeta(-z) = -\zeta(z)$. Here `L.weierstrassZeta` is the Weierstrass $\zeta$ function of $\Lambda$, $\zeta(z) = \frac{1}{z} + \sum_{l \in \Lambda,\ l \neq 0} \left(\frac{1}{z - l} + \frac{1}{l} + \frac{z}{l^2}\right)$.

This is the classical oddness of $\zeta$, with the classical normalisation of the series. The reason is the symmetry $\Lambda = -\Lambda$: the substitution $l \mapsto -l$ permutes the nonzero lattice points and turns each term of the series for $\zeta(-z)$ into minus a term of the series for $\zeta(z)$, while $\frac{1}{-z} = -\frac{1}{z}$.

## What it says
The Weierstrass $\zeta$ function is quasi-periodic: a shift of the argument by a lattice vector changes it by a constant. Here this takes the form $\zeta(z - l) = \zeta(z) - \eta(l)$.

- `(L : PeriodPair)`: a period pair, two complex numbers that are linearly independent over $\mathbb{R}$. Their integer combinations form the lattice $\Lambda$, `L.lattice`.
- `(z : ℂ)`: a complex number, with no condition on it.
- `(l : ↥L.lattice)`: an element $l$ of the lattice $\Lambda$. In the statement `↑l` is $l$ seen as a complex number.
- The conclusion: `L.weierstrassZeta (z - ↑l) = L.weierstrassZeta z - L.quasiPeriod l`, that is $\zeta(z - l) = \zeta(z) - \eta(l)$. Here $\zeta$ is the Weierstrass $\zeta$ function of $\Lambda$, $\zeta(z) = \frac{1}{z} + \sum_{l \in \Lambda,\ l \neq 0} \left(\frac{1}{z - l} + \frac{1}{l} + \frac{z}{l^2}\right)$, and $\eta$, `L.quasiPeriod`, is its quasi-period map: the additive map from $\Lambda$ to $\mathbb{C}$ for which $\eta(l)$ is the constant value of $\zeta(z + l) - \zeta(z)$.

This is the classical quasi-periodicity $\zeta(w + l) = \zeta(w) + \eta(l)$ (in Tau Ceti `PeriodPair.weierstrassZeta_add_coe`), applied at $w = z - l$. The statement is the classical one, for every lattice vector $l$.

## What it says
For a character $\chi$ of $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times$ with values in $\mathbb{C}^\times$, this is the field $\mathbb{Q}(\chi)$: the subfield of $\mathbb{C}$ generated over $\mathbb{Q}$ by the values of $\chi$.

- `(χ : (ZMod N)ˣ →* ℂˣ)`: a group homomorphism $\chi$ from the units of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ to the nonzero complex numbers, for a natural number $N$ that Lean reads off from $\chi$. In the modular forms files it is the nebentypus character of a form of level $N$.
- The value: `IntermediateField.adjoin ℚ (Set.range fun u : (ZMod N)ˣ => (χ u : ℂ))`, the smallest subfield of $\mathbb{C}$ that contains $\mathbb{Q}$ and every value $\chi(u)$ for $u \in (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times$, as a field between $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{C}$.

This is the standard field of values $\mathbb{Q}(\chi)$ of a Dirichlet character. A Dirichlet character is often taken on all of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$, extended by $0$ off the units. That adds only the value $0$, which lies in every field, so the field is the same.

## What it says
For a newform $f$ of level $N$ and weight $k$, this is its coefficient field: the subfield of $\mathbb{C}$ generated over $\mathbb{Q}$ by its Fourier coefficients $a_n(f)$, $n \geq 1$.

- `[NeZero N]`: the level $N$, a natural number, is not $0$.
- `(f : HeckeRing.GL2.Newform N k)`: a newform $f$ of level $N$ and integer weight $k$. That is a nonzero cusp form on $\Gamma_1(N)$ with a nebentypus character, an eigenform of the Hecke operators away from the level, lying in the new subspace and normalised by $a_1 = 1$; the docstring of `HeckeRing.GL2.Newform` calls it Miyake's primitive form.
- The value: `IntermediateField.adjoin ℚ (Set.range fun n : ℕ+ => (qExpansion 1 f.toCuspForm).coeff (n : ℕ))`, the smallest subfield of $\mathbb{C}$ that contains $\mathbb{Q}$ and every coefficient $a_n(f)$, $n \geq 1$, of the $q$-expansion $f = \sum_n a_n(f) q^n$, $q = e^{2\pi i \tau}$.

This is the standard coefficient field $\mathbb{Q}(a_n(f) : n \geq 1)$ of a newform. Leaving out $a_0$ changes nothing: $f$ is a cusp form, so $a_0(f) = 0$, which lies in every field.

## What it says
The level-raising, or degeneracy, operator $V_d$. It sends a cusp form $f$ of weight $k$ for a group $\mathcal{G}$ to the cusp form $\tau \mapsto f(d\tau)$ for a smaller group $\mathcal{G}'$.

- `[𝒢'.HasDetOne]`: the target group $\mathcal{G}'$, a subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$, lies in $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$.
- `(d : ℕ)`: a natural number $d$, the factor by which the argument is scaled.
- `[NeZero d]`: $d \neq 0$.
- `(h : 𝒢' ≤ ConjAct.toConjAct (scaleGL d)⁻¹ • 𝒢)`: $\mathcal{G}'$ lies in the conjugate group $\alpha_d^{-1}\mathcal{G}\alpha_d$, where $\alpha_d = \begin{pmatrix} d & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ is `scaleGL d`.
- `(f : CuspForm 𝒢 k)`: a cusp form $f$ of integer weight $k$ for the subgroup $\mathcal{G}$ of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$.
- The value: `((d : ℂ) ^ (1 - k)) • CuspForm.restrict h (CuspForm.translate f (scaleGL d))`. This is $d^{1-k}$ times the slash $f|_k\alpha_d$, a cusp form for $\alpha_d^{-1}\mathcal{G}\alpha_d$, read as a cusp form for $\mathcal{G}'$. The slash is $d^{k-1}f(d\tau)$, so the value is the function $\tau \mapsto f(d\tau)$.

This is the classical operator $f(\tau) \mapsto f(d\tau)$, with no power of $d$ in front. For $f$ on $\Gamma_1(M)$ it gives a form on $\Gamma_1(dM)$, and the images of such maps span the old subspace.

## What it says
The Eisenstein series $G_k^{\psi,\varphi}$ with characters $\psi$ modulo $u$ and $\varphi$ modulo $v$, as a modular form of weight $k \geq 3$ on $\Gamma_1(N)$ when $uv \mid N$. It is the function $z \mapsto \sum_{(m,n) \in \mathbb{Z}^2,\ v \mid m} \psi(m/v)\,\bar\varphi(n)\,(mz+n)^{-k}$ on the upper half-plane.

- `(ψ : DirichletCharacter ℂ u)`: a Dirichlet character $\psi$ modulo a natural number $u$, with complex values.
- `(φ : DirichletCharacter ℂ v)`: a Dirichlet character $\varphi$ modulo a natural number $v$, with complex values.
- `[NeZero N]`: the level $N$, a natural number, is not $0$.
- `(hk : 3 ≤ k)`: the weight $k$, an integer, is at least $3$.
- `(huv : u * v ∣ N)`: $uv$ divides $N$.
- The value: the Eisenstein series of level $\Gamma(N)$ that weights each pair $(m, n)$ by a function of its residues modulo $N$, here `charWeight N ψ φ`, read as a modular form for $\Gamma_1(N)$ once it is shown to be invariant under $\Gamma_1(N)$. Its value at $z$ is the series above, which does not involve $N$.

This is the series $G_k^{\psi,\varphi}$ of Diamond–Shurman §4.5, written as a single sum over $\mathbb{Z}^2$: the condition $v \mid m$ and the factor $\psi(m/v)$ stand for the sum over pairs $(cv, d)$ with weight $\psi(c)\bar\varphi(d)$. It is the raw series, not the normalised one: for primitive $\varphi$ it is a nonzero constant times the series whose coefficients are the twisted divisor sums.

## References and tests

- `TauCeti.EisensteinSeries.charEisensteinSeriesMF_mem_modFormCharSpace` — it lies in $M_k(N, \psi\varphi)$: its nebentypus is $\psi\varphi$, both characters lifted to modulus $N$.
- `TauCeti.EisensteinSeries.charEisensteinSeriesMF_eq_zero` — it is $0$ when $\psi(-1)\varphi(-1) \neq (-1)^k$.
- `TauCeti.EisensteinSeries.qExpansion_charEisensteinSeriesMF_coeff_of_isPrimitive` — for primitive $\varphi$ and $\psi(-1)\varphi(-1) = (-1)^k$, its $n$-th coefficient, $n \geq 1$, is $\frac{2(-2\pi i)^k}{(k-1)!\,v^k}\, g(\varphi^{-1})$ times the twisted divisor sum $\sum_{d \mid n} \psi(n/d)\varphi(d)d^{k-1}$.

Together the tests show that the definition is the lattice sum of the literature, with the expected nebentypus $\psi\varphi$, that it vanishes for the wrong parity as the classical series does, and that its coefficients are the classical ones, with the classical Gauss-sum constant.

## What it says
A $2 \times 2$ integer matrix $M$ is an Atkin–Lehner matrix for $Q$ at level $N$ when it has the shape $\begin{pmatrix} Qa & b \\ Nc & Qd \end{pmatrix}$ with $a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{Z}$ and determinant $Q$.

- `(N Q : ℕ)`: the level $N$ and the divisor $Q$, natural numbers; the predicate asks nothing of them.
- `(M : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℤ)`: a $2 \times 2$ matrix with integer entries, its rows and columns indexed by $0$ and $1$.
- The value is a proposition, true when its four fields hold:
  - `dvd_apply_zero_zero`: $Q$ divides the upper-left entry `M 0 0`;
  - `dvd_apply_one_zero`: $N$ divides the lower-left entry `M 1 0`;
  - `dvd_apply_one_one`: $Q$ divides the lower-right entry `M 1 1`;
  - `det_eq`: $\det M = Q$.

The upper-right entry is free. Writing the divisibilities as $M_{00} = Qa$, $M_{10} = Nc$, $M_{11} = Qd$ gives the docstring's matrix, with $\det M = Q^2 ad - Nbc = Q$. This is the standard notion: for an exact divisor $Q$ of $N$, the Atkin–Lehner involution $W_Q$ is the action of any matrix of this shape, and such matrices differ from one another by elements of $\Gamma_0(N)$. The predicate itself does not ask that $Q \mid N$, that $\gcd(Q, N/Q) = 1$ or that $Q > 0$: it describes the matrices, and the results that use it assume what they need.

## What it says
Two modular forms of the same weight $k$ for a group $\mathcal{G}$ that meets $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ in a subgroup of finite index $m$ are equal as soon as their $q$-expansions at $\infty$ agree in every coefficient of index $i \le \lfloor km/12 \rfloor$. This is Sturm's bound, in the form that decides equality.

- `[𝒢.IsFiniteRelIndex (Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup.mapGL ℝ).range]`: $\mathcal{G}$, a subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ given implicitly, meets the copy $\mathcal{SL}$ of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ inside $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ in a subgroup of finite index $m = [\mathcal{SL} : \mathcal{G} \cap \mathcal{SL}]$. The weight $k$ is an integer, also implicit.
- `(f : ModularForm 𝒢 k)`: a modular form $f$ of weight $k$ for $\mathcal{G}$: holomorphic on the upper half plane, invariant under the weight-$k$ action of $\mathcal{G}$, and bounded at the cusps.
- `[DiscreteTopology ↥𝒢.strictPeriods]`: the strict periods of $\mathcal{G}$, the real $x$ with $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & x \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in \mathcal{G}$, form a discrete subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$, so they are $w\mathbb{Z}$ for the strict width $w > 0$ of the cusp $\infty$.
- `(g : ModularForm 𝒢 k)`: a second modular form $g$, of the same weight for the same group.
- `(h : ∀ i ≤ (k * ↑(Nat.card (↥(Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup.mapGL ℝ).range ⧸ 𝒢.subgroupOf (Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup.mapGL ℝ).range))).toNat / 12, (PowerSeries.coeff i) (UpperHalfPlane.qExpansion 𝒢.strictWidthInfty ⇑f) = (PowerSeries.coeff i) (UpperHalfPlane.qExpansion 𝒢.strictWidthInfty ⇑g))`: for every natural number $i \le \lfloor km/12 \rfloor$, the coefficient of $q_w^i$ in the expansion of $f$ in $q_w = e^{2\pi i \tau/w}$ equals that of $g$.
- The conclusion: $f = g$.

Sturm's theorem says that a form for a subgroup of index $m$ in $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ whose expansion at $\infty$ vanishes beyond order $km/12$ is zero; applied to $f - g$ it gives this. The group may be any subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ meeting $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ in finite index, which covers every congruence subgroup. For $\Gamma_1(N)$ the width is $1$ and $m = [\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z}) : \Gamma_1(N)]$.

The definition therefore asks $\sigma(x) > 0$ for every real embedding $\sigma$, which is the standard notion of a totally positive element. - `(hq : ∀ m ∈ f.newtonSlopes v, m = ↑q)`: every slope of the Newton polygon of $f$ with respect to $v$, the slopes of its finite edges counted with multiplicity, equals the rational number $q$.
- `(hden : q.den = f.natDegree)`: the denominator of $q$ in lowest terms equals the degree of $f$.
- The conclusion: `Irreducible f`, $f$ is not a unit, and whenever $f = gh$ one of $g$, $h$ is a unit, that is, a nonzero constant.

This is the classical criterion of Eisenstein–Dumas type: the degree of any factor is a multiple of the denominator of $q$, which is $\deg f$, so a factor has degree $0$ or $\deg f$.

In the literature the action is $\rho(t) = t^2 \operatorname{Ad} \lambda(t^{-1})$ for a cocharacter $\lambda$ with differential $h$, and $\operatorname{Ad} \lambda(t)(e) = t^2 e$ gives the same conclusion: $e$ is the fixed point to which the action contracts the Slodowy slice.

- `Kˣ` is the group of nonzero elements of $K$; the action is not defined at $c = 0$.
- `t.contractingAction c` is a linear map $L \to L$, here applied to $e$.
- The result holds over any field of characteristic $0$; no algebraic group is involved, the action being defined by its eigenspace formula.

## What it says
The contracting action attached to an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple $(h, e, f)$ maps the Slodowy slice $e + \ker(\operatorname{ad} f)$ into itself.

- `[Field K] [CharZero K]`: $K$ is a field of characteristic $0$.
- `[LieRing L] [LieAlgebra K L]`: $L$ is a Lie algebra over $K$.
- `[FiniteDimensional K L]`: $L$ is finite-dimensional over $K$.
- `(t : IsSl2Triple h e f)`: $h, e, f \in L$ form an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple: $[e, f] = h$, $[h, e] = 2e$, $[h, f] = -2f$, with $h \neq 0$.
- `(c : Kˣ)`: a nonzero scalar $c \in K$.
- `(hx : x ∈ TauCeti.slodowySlice K e f)`: $x$ lies in the Slodowy slice, the affine subspace $e + \ker(\operatorname{ad} f)$ of the $e + z$ with $[f, z] = 0$.
- The conclusion: `(t.contractingAction c) x` lies in the slice too, where $\rho(c)$ = `t.contractingAction c` multiplies the $j$-eigenspace of $\operatorname{ad} h$ by $c^{2-j}$.

This is the standard fact behind the contracting action on the slice: $\rho(c)$ fixes $e$, and it preserves $\ker(\operatorname{ad} f)$, which is stable under $\operatorname{ad} h$ (because $[h, f] = -2f$) and so is the sum of its intersections with the eigenspaces of $\operatorname{ad} h$. Hence $\rho(c)(e + z) = e + \rho(c)(z)$ stays in $e + \ker(\operatorname{ad} f)$. In $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ itself, $\rho(c)(e + af) = e + c^4 a f$.

## Lean subtleties

- The action is defined by its eigenspace formula, with no algebraic group, so the result holds over any field of characteristic $0$.

## What it says
The weights of the contracting action attached to an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple $(h, e, f)$: a nonzero scalar $c$ acts on the $j$-eigenspace of $\operatorname{ad} h$ by multiplication by $c^{2 - j}$.

- `[Field K] [CharZero K]`: $K$ is a field of characteristic $0$.
- `[LieRing L] [LieAlgebra K L]`: $L$ is a Lie algebra over $K$.
- `[FiniteDimensional K L]`: $L$ is finite-dimensional over $K$.
- `(t : IsSl2Triple h e f)`: $h, e, f \in L$ form an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple: $[e, f] = h$, $[h, e] = 2e$, $[h, f] = -2f$, with $h \neq 0$.
- `(c : Kˣ)`: a nonzero scalar $c \in K$.
- `(hx : x ∈ ((LieAlgebra.ad K L) h).eigenspace ↑j)`: for an integer $j$, $x \in L$ satisfies $[h, x] = j x$, that is, $x$ lies in the $j$-eigenspace $L(j)$ of $\operatorname{ad} h$ (with $x = 0$ allowed).
- The conclusion: `(t.contractingAction c) x = ↑c ^ (2 - j) • x`, the contracting action $\rho(c)$ sends $x$ to $c^{2-j} x$.

This is the weight computation for the standard contracting action $\rho(t) = t^2 \operatorname{Ad} \lambda(t^{-1})$ of the literature, $\lambda$ a cocharacter with differential $h$: $\operatorname{Ad} \lambda(t^{-1})$ acts on $L(j)$ by $t^{-j}$. Here it recovers the definition, $c^2$ times the grading automorphism at $c^{-1}$, eigenspace by eigenspace. For instance $e$ ($j = 2$) is fixed, $h$ ($j = 0$) is scaled by $c^2$, and $f$ ($j = -2$) by $c^4$.

- `↑j` casts the integer $j$ into $K$; in characteristic $0$ distinct integers stay distinct, so distinct $j$ give distinct eigenspaces.
- If $j$ is not an eigenvalue of $\operatorname{ad} h$, the eigenspace is $0$ and the statement says nothing.
- `•` is multiplication of a vector by a scalar.

## What it says
The contracting action extends to $c = 0$ on the Slodowy slice: a point $x$ of $e + \ker(\operatorname{ad} f)$ is $e + \sum_n v_n$ with $v_n \in \ker(\operatorname{ad} f)$ of weight $-n$ for $\operatorname{ad} h$, and a nonzero $c$ moves it to $e + \sum_n c^{n+2} v_n$, a polynomial in $c$ with value $e$ at $c = 0$.

- `[Field K] [CharZero K]`: $K$ is a field of characteristic $0$.
- `[LieRing L] [LieAlgebra K L]`: $L$ is a Lie algebra over $K$.
- `[FiniteDimensional K L]`: $L$ is finite-dimensional over $K$.
- `(t : IsSl2Triple h e f)`: $h, e, f \in L$ form an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple: $[e, f] = h$, $[h, e] = 2e$, $[h, f] = -2f$, with $h \neq 0$.
- `(hx : x ∈ TauCeti.slodowySlice K e f)`: $x$ lies in the Slodowy slice, the affine subspace $e + \ker(\operatorname{ad} f)$ of $L$.
- The conclusion: there is a finitely supported family $(v_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of elements of $L$ such that each $v_n$ commutes with $f$ and satisfies $[h, v_n] = -n v_n$; $x = e + \sum_n v_n$; and for every nonzero $c \in K$ the contracting action $\rho(c)$ sends $x$ to $e + \sum_n c^{n+2} v_n$.

This is the algebraic form of the standard fact that the action $\rho(t) = t^2 \operatorname{Ad} \lambda(t^{-1})$ contracts the slice to $e$: $\rho(t)(x) \to e$ as $t \to 0$. It rests on $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-representation theory: $\ker(\operatorname{ad} f)$ consists of lowest-weight vectors, whose $\operatorname{ad} h$-eigenvalues are $0, -1, -2, \dots$, and $\rho(c)$ acts on weight $-n$ by $c^{2-(-n)} = c^{n+2}$. All the weights $n + 2$ of the action on the slice are positive.

- `ℕ →₀ L` is a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $L$ that vanishes outside a finite set, and `v.sum fun n w => …` is the finite sum over the $n$ where $v_n \neq 0$.
- `⊓` of two subspaces is their intersection; `eigenspace (-↑n)` is the eigenspace of $\operatorname{ad} h$ for the eigenvalue $-n$, the natural number $n$ cast into $K$.
- The action is defined only for nonzero $c$ (`Kˣ`); the extension to $c = 0$ is read off the formula, whose exponents $n + 2 \ge 2$ are natural numbers. Over a general field of characteristic $0$ there is no limit in a topological sense, and the polynomial formula takes its place.

## What it says
Any two regular elements $x$ and $y$ of a Lie algebra $L$ over a field $K$ have centralizers of the same dimension.

- `[Field K]`: $K$ is a field.
- `[LieRing L] [LieAlgebra K L]`: $L$ is a Lie algebra over $K$, of any dimension.
- `(hx : IsCentralizerRegular K x)`: $x \in L$ is regular: its centralizer $\ker(\operatorname{ad} x) = \{z \in L : [x, z] = 0\}$ has the least dimension among the centralizers of all elements of $L$.
- `(hy : IsCentralizerRegular K y)`: $y \in L$ is regular in the same sense.
- The conclusion: `Module.finrank K ↥(LinearMap.ker ((ad K L) x))`, the dimension of the centralizer of $x$, equals that of the centralizer of $y$.

With regularity defined by minimal centralizer dimension, this says that the minimum is one number shared by all regular elements: for a reductive Lie algebra this common dimension is the rank. It is the expected basic property of the definition, and needs no hypothesis on $K$ or on the dimension of $L$.

## What it says
In a finite-dimensional Lie algebra $L$ over a field $K$, fix a regular element $x_0$, one whose centralizer has the least possible dimension. Then an element $x$ is regular exactly when the image of $\operatorname{ad} x$ has dimension at least that of the image of $\operatorname{ad} x_0$.

- `[Field K]`: $K$ is a field, of any characteristic.
- `[LieRing L] [LieAlgebra K L]`: $L$ is a Lie algebra over $K$, with bracket $[\cdot,\cdot]$.
- `[FiniteDimensional K L]`: $L$ has finite dimension over $K$.
- `(hx₀ : IsCentralizerRegular K x₀)`: the element $x_0 \in L$ is regular: its centralizer $\ker(\operatorname{ad} x_0) = \{y \in L : [x_0, y] = 0\}$ has the least dimension among the centralizers of all elements of $L$.
- The conclusion: for every $x \in L$, `IsCentralizerRegular K x` holds if and only if $\dim_K \operatorname{im}(\operatorname{ad} x_0) \le \dim_K \operatorname{im}(\operatorname{ad} x)$. Here `ad K L x` is the linear map $\operatorname{ad} x : L \to L$, $y \mapsto [x, y]$, `LinearMap.range` is its image and `Module.finrank` the dimension.

By rank–nullity, $\dim \ker(\operatorname{ad} x) + \dim \operatorname{im}(\operatorname{ad} x) = \dim L$, so the elements whose centralizer has least dimension are those for which $\operatorname{ad} x$ has the greatest rank, and that greatest rank is the rank of $\operatorname{ad} x_0$. This is the standard description of the regular elements as those at which $\operatorname{ad}$ has maximal rank, with one regular element $x_0$ as the yardstick.

## What it says

## What it says

This is the standard openness of the regular set.

In a finite-dimensional Lie algebra $L$ over an infinite field $K$, written in coordinates by a basis, the regular elements are Zariski-dense: the only polynomial vanishing at the coordinates of every regular element is $0$.

This is the standard density of the regular elements, here over any infinite field.

## What it says
Cyclic cochains compute the cohomology of the cyclic bicomplex in degree $m$, once $1, 2, \dots, m$ are invertible in the ring of scalars.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring, the ring of scalars.
- `[NonUnitalSemiring A] [Module R A] [IsScalarTower R A A] [SMulCommClass R A A]`: $A$ is an associative $R$-algebra, not necessarily with a $1$: an $R$-module with an associative product that is $R$-bilinear, $(ra)b = r(ab) = a(rb)$.

- `(m : ℕ)`: the cohomological degree $m$.
- `(hR : ∀ q < m, IsUnit (↑q + 1))`: for every natural number $q < m$, the element $q + 1$ of $R$ is a unit; that is, $1, 2, \dots, m$ are invertible in $R$, or equivalently $m!$ is.
- The conclusion: `cyclicCochainComplexToTotal R A M`, the cochain map from Connes' cyclic cochain complex $C_\lambda^\bullet$ (the cyclic $M$-valued cochains on $A$, with the Hochschild coboundary $b$) to the total complex of the cyclic bicomplex, which puts cyclic cochains in column zero, is a quasi-isomorphism in degree $m$: it induces an isomorphism $H^m(C_\lambda^\bullet) \cong H^m(\mathrm{Tot})$.

This is the standard comparison of Connes' complex with the cyclic bicomplex. Row $q$ of the bicomplex is exact away from column zero once $q + 1$ is invertible, and in total degrees $m$ and $m - 1$ the entries outside column zero lie in rows $q < m$, so $1, \dots, m$ invertible suffices. Over a ring containing $\mathbb{Q}$ the hypothesis holds in every degree.

## What it says
A natural number $p$ is a common index divisor of a number field $K$ when it divides the index $[\mathcal{O}_K : \mathbb{Z}[\theta]]$ of every integral primitive element $\theta$ of $K$.

Equivalently, $p$ divides the gcd of all the indices $i(\theta)$. For a prime $p$ this is the classical notion of a common index divisor, or inessential prime, of $K$; for other $p$ it is the same condition, read as a common divisor of the indices. A common index divisor other than $1$ rules out a power integral basis, which is why it obstructs monogenicity.

## What it says

- The norm of $H^2$ is that of $L^2$ of the circle for Haar measure of total mass $1$, so $\|x\|^2 = \sum_n |\hat{x}(n)|^2$; another normalisation of the measure would rescale the value.
- `‖↑w‖` is the absolute value $|w|$ of $w$ as a complex number, and `√` is the real square root. On the open disk $1 - |w|^2$ lies in $(0, 1]$, so the square root and its inverse are the true ones, with no junk value; at $w = 0$ the norm is $1$, that of $x \mapsto \hat{x}(0)$.

## What it says
The Szegő kernel $k_w$ of the Hardy space $H^2$ at a point $w$ of the open unit disk has norm $(1 - |w|^2)^{-1/2}$.

- `(w : ↑(Metric.ball 0 1))`: a point $w \in \mathbb{C}$ with $|w| < 1$.
- The conclusion: the norm of `reproducingKernel w`, the Szegő kernel at $w$ as an element of the boundary Hardy space, equals $(\sqrt{1 - |w|^2})^{-1}$, the reciprocal square root of $1 - |w|^2$.

This is the standard value for arc length normalised to total mass $1$. The kernel $k_w(z) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \bar{w}^n z^n$ has Fourier coefficients $\bar{w}^n$, so by Parseval
$$\|k_w\|^2 = \sum_{n \ge 0} |w|^{2n} = \frac{1}{1 - |w|^2}.$$
For instance $\|k_0\| = 1$ and $\|k_{1/2}\|^2 = 4/3$.

## What it says
The squared norm of the Szegő kernel $k_w$ of the Hardy space $H^2$, at a point $w$ of the open unit disk, is $1/(1 - |w|^2)$.

- `(w : ↑(Metric.ball 0 1))`: a point $w \in \mathbb{C}$ with $|w| < 1$.
- The conclusion: the square of the norm of `reproducingKernel w`, the Szegő kernel at $w$ as an element of the boundary Hardy space, equals $(1 - |w|^2)^{-1}$.

This is the standard value $\langle k_w, k_w \rangle = k_w(w) = 1/(1 - |w|^2)$ for the circle with normalised measure $d\theta / 2\pi$. It follows from the reproducing property applied to $k_w$ itself, together with the closed form $k_w(z) = 1/(1 - \bar{w} z)$ at $z = w$; equally, from Parseval, $\sum_{n \ge 0} |\bar{w}^n|^2 = \sum_{n \ge 0} |w|^{2n}$. For instance, at $w = 1/2$ it is $4/3$, and at $w = 0$ it is $1$, the squared norm of the constant function $1$.

## What it says
A nonnegative square matrix of positive order can be scaled by strictly positive row and column factors to a doubly stochastic matrix if and only if it has total support.

- `[Fintype n] [DecidableEq n] [Nonempty n]`: $n$ is a finite, nonempty index set with decidable equality, so the matrices are $N \times N$ with $N = |n| \ge 1$.
- `(hK : ∀ (i j : n), 0 ≤ K i j)`: the real matrix $K$, given implicitly, has nonnegative entries.
- The conclusion: there are vectors $u, v \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $u_i > 0$ and $v_j > 0$ for all $i, j$ such that the matrix with entries $u_i K_{ij} v_j$, that is $D_u K D_v$ for the diagonal matrices $D_u$ and $D_v$, lies in `doublyStochastic ℝ n` (nonnegative entries, every row sum and every column sum equal to $1$), if and only if $K$ satisfies `K.HasTotalSupport`: $K \ne 0$ and every nonzero entry of $K$ lies on a permutation diagonal of nonzero entries, that is $K_{i\sigma(i)} \ne 0$ for all $i$, for some permutation $\sigma$ with $\sigma(i_0) = j_0$ given the entry $(i_0, j_0)$.

This is the Sinkhorn–Knopp criterion for doubly stochastic scaling, with the same hypotheses: nonnegative real entries and positive diagonal scalings.

## What it says
For an exponent $p \in [1, \infty]$ and a metric space $Z$, the Gromov–Wasserstein space of $Z$-valued measured kernels is a geodesic space, provided every coupling of two kernels carries a measurable family of geodesics of $Z$ joining the paired kernel values.

- `[MetricSpace Z]`: $Z$ is a metric space, in which the kernels take their values.
- `[Fact (1 ≤ p)]`: the exponent $p$, an element of `ENNReal` $= [0, \infty]$, satisfies $1 \le p$; $p = \infty$ is allowed.
- `(h : ∀ (K L : GromovWassersteinPresentation p Z) (π : MeasureTheory.Measure (K.Carrier × L.Carrier)), IsCoupling π K.measure L.measure → ∃ (g : (K.Carrier × L.Carrier) × K.Carrier × L.Carrier → ℝ → Z), (∀ᵐ (q : (K.Carrier × L.Carrier) × K.Carrier × L.Carrier) ∂π.prod π, IsGeodesicSegment (g q) (K.kernel (q.1.1, q.2.1)) (L.kernel (q.1.2, q.2.2))) ∧ ∀ t ∈ Set.Icc 0 1, MeasureTheory.AEStronglyMeasurable (fun (q : (K.Carrier × L.Carrier) × K.Carrier × L.Carrier) => g q t) (π.prod π))`: the hypothesis `h`. Take two presentations $K$ and $L$, each a standard Borel probability space $(X, \mu)$ with a kernel $\omega : X \times X \to Z$ of finite $p$-size, and a coupling $\pi$ of $\mu_K$ and $\mu_L$: a measure on $X_K \times X_L$ with these two marginals. Then there are curves $g_q : \mathbb{R} \to Z$, one for each pair $q = ((x, y), (x', y'))$ of points of $X_K \times X_L$, such that for $\pi \otimes \pi$-almost every $q$ the curve $g_q$ is, on $[0, 1]$, a constant-speed geodesic from $\omega_K(x, x')$ to $\omega_L(y, y')$, and for each $t \in [0, 1]$ the map $q \mapsto g_q(t)$ is almost everywhere strongly measurable for $\pi \otimes \pi$.
- The conclusion: `IsGeodesicSpace (GromovWassersteinSpace p Z)`: any two points of the Gromov–Wasserstein space, the finite-size standard Borel measured kernels modulo weak isomorphism with the Gromov–Wasserstein metric, are joined by a geodesic segment.

This is the standard argument that the space is geodesic, with its one non-constructive step, a measurable choice of geodesics, made a hypothesis: over an optimal coupling, the kernels $q \mapsto g_q(t)$ interpolate between $K$ and $L$, and their classes form a geodesic segment, as the docstring says. The name says openly that the choice is assumed.

## What it says
A measure $\nu$ on $X$ has finite $p$-th moment when, for some base point $x$, the distance $y \mapsto d(x, y)$ lies in $L^p(\nu)$.

- `[MeasurableSpace X]`: a σ-algebra on the type $X$, on which measures live.
- `[EDist X]`: an extended distance $d : X \times X \to [0, \infty]$ on $X$. No axioms are asked of it here; the docstring has an extended pseudometric space in mind.
- `(p : ENNReal)`: the exponent $p \in [0, \infty]$.
- `(ν : MeasureTheory.Measure X)`: a measure $\nu$ on $X$, not necessarily finite.

Its value is `∃ x : X, MemLp (fun y ↦ edist x y) p ν`: there is a point $x \in X$ such that $y \mapsto d(x, y)$ is almost everywhere strongly measurable for $\nu$ and has finite $L^p$ norm. For $0 < p < \infty$ this says $\int d(x, y)^p \, d\nu(y) < \infty$; for $p = \infty$, that $d(x, \cdot)$ is $\nu$-essentially bounded.

For $1 \le p < \infty$ and a probability measure on a metric space, this is the condition that defines the Wasserstein space $P_p(X)$: $\int d(x_0, y)^p \, d\nu(y) < \infty$ for some, hence every, base point $x_0$. The definition allows any measure and any extended distance, and asks for one base point.

## What it says
If two measures on a pseudometric space have finite $p$-th moment and one of them is finite, their sum has finite $p$-th moment.

- `[MeasurableSpace X]`: a σ-algebra on the type $X$; $p \in [0, \infty]$ is the exponent, and $\mu$, $\nu$ are measures on $X$.
- `[PseudoMetricSpace X] [OpensMeasurableSpace X]`: $X$ carries a pseudometric (a metric in which distinct points may be at distance $0$), and every open set is measurable.
- `[MeasureTheory.IsFiniteMeasure ν]`: $\nu(X) < \infty$. Nothing of the kind is asked of $\mu$.
- `(hμ : HasFiniteMoment p μ)`: for some base point $x$, the distance $y \mapsto d(x, y)$ lies in $L^p(\mu)$.
- `(hν : HasFiniteMoment p ν)`: the same for $\nu$, perhaps about another base point.
- The conclusion: `HasFiniteMoment p (μ + ν)`: about some base point, the distance function lies in $L^p(\mu + \nu)$.

This is the closure of the finite-moment measures under addition. One measure must be finite: a finite measure with finite moment has it about every base point, so both witnesses can be taken about the base point of $\mu$. Without that hypothesis the statement fails: on $\mathbb{R}$ with $p = 1$, $\sum_n \delta_{1/n^2}$ has finite moment about $0$ and $\sum_n \delta_{1 + 1/n^2}$ about $1$, but their sum has finite moment about no point.

## What it says
On a pseudometric space, every real Lipschitz function is integrable against a finite measure with finite first moment.

- `[MeasurableSpace X] [PseudoMetricSpace X] [OpensMeasurableSpace X]`: $X$ is a pseudometric space with a σ-algebra in which every open set is measurable.
- `[MeasureTheory.IsFiniteMeasure ν]`: $\nu$ is a measure on $X$ with $\nu(X) < \infty$.
- `(h : HasFiniteMoment 1 ν)`: $\nu$ has finite first moment: $\int d(x_0, y) \, d\nu(y) < \infty$ for some base point $x_0$.
- `(hf : LipschitzWith K f)`: $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is Lipschitz with constant $K \ge 0$: $|f(x) - f(y)| \le K \, d(x, y)$ for all $x, y$.
- The conclusion: `MeasureTheory.Integrable f ν`: $f$ is measurable and $\int |f| \, d\nu < \infty$.

The reason is the bound $|f(y)| \le |f(x_0)| + K \, d(x_0, y)$: the finite mass integrates the constant, and the first moment integrates the distance. As the docstring says, these $f$ are the test functions of the Kantorovich–Rubinstein formula for $W_1$, so the statement makes their integrals meaningful for every finite measure of finite first moment. Both hypotheses on $\nu$ are needed: a nonzero constant is Lipschitz and is integrable only against a finite measure, and the test below shows a probability measure against which a Lipschitz function is not integrable.

## What it says
The pushforward of a measure with finite $p$-th moment under a measurable Lipschitz map has finite $p$-th moment.

- `[MeasurableSpace X] [MeasurableSpace Y]`: σ-algebras on the types $X$ and $Y$. The implicit $\mu$ is a measure on $X$, $f : X \to Y$ a map, $p \in [0, \infty]$ the exponent and $K \ge 0$ a constant.
- `[PseudoEMetricSpace X] [PseudoEMetricSpace Y]`: $X$ and $Y$ are extended pseudometric spaces: distances lie in $[0, \infty]$, and distinct points may be at distance $0$.
- `(hμ : HasFiniteMoment p μ)`: $\mu$ has finite $p$-th moment: for some $x_0 \in X$, the distance $y \mapsto d(x_0, y)$ lies in $L^p(\mu)$.
- `(hdY : ∀ (y : Y), Measurable fun (z : Y) => edist y z)`: on $Y$, every distance function $z \mapsto d(y, z)$ is measurable.
- `(hf : Measurable f)`: $f$ is measurable.
- `(hLip : LipschitzWith K f)`: $f$ is $K$-Lipschitz: $d(f(x), f(x')) \le K \, d(x, x')$.
- The conclusion: `HasFiniteMoment p (MeasureTheory.Measure.map f μ)`: the pushforward $f_*\mu$, given by $(f_*\mu)(B) = \mu(f^{-1}(B))$, has finite $p$-th moment.

The base point is carried along: if $d(x_0, \cdot) \in L^p(\mu)$, then $d(f(x_0), \cdot) \in L^p(f_*\mu)$, since for $0 < p < \infty$, $\int d(f(x_0), z)^p \, d(f_*\mu)(z) = \int d(f(x_0), f(y))^p \, d\mu(y) \le K^p \int d(x_0, y)^p \, d\mu(y)$. As the same base point serves throughout, $\mu$ need not be finite. This is the standard stability of finite moments under Lipschitz maps.

## What it says
On a pseudometric space, a finite measure with finite $p$-th moment about some base point has it about every base point whose distance function is measurable.

- `[MeasurableSpace X]`: a σ-algebra on the type $X$. The implicit $p \in [0, \infty]$ is the exponent and $\nu$ a measure on $X$.
- `[PseudoMetricSpace X]`: $X$ carries a pseudometric $d$, with finite values; distinct points may be at distance $0$.
- `(h : HasFiniteMoment p ν)`: $\nu$ has finite $p$-th moment: for some base point $x_0$, the distance $y \mapsto d(x_0, y)$ lies in $L^p(\nu)$.
- `(hd : MeasureTheory.AEStronglyMeasurable (fun (y : X) => edist x y) ν)`: for the given point $x$, the distance function $y \mapsto d(x, y)$ is almost everywhere strongly measurable for $\nu$: it agrees $\nu$-almost everywhere with a limit of simple functions.
- `[MeasureTheory.IsFiniteMeasure ν]`: $\nu(X) < \infty$.
- The conclusion: `MeasureTheory.MemLp (fun (y : X) => edist x y) p ν`: $y \mapsto d(x, y)$ lies in $L^p(\nu)$; for $0 < p < \infty$, $\int d(x, y)^p \, d\nu(y) < \infty$.

This is the independence of the base point in the moment condition that defines the Wasserstein space $P_p(X)$. It follows from $d(x, y) \le d(x, x_0) + d(x_0, y)$, the constant $d(x, x_0)$ lying in $L^p(\nu)$ because $\nu$ is finite. The two further hypotheses are needed: measurability, since no compatibility between the σ-algebra and the metric is assumed, and finiteness, since a nonzero constant is not in $L^p$ of an infinite measure.

## What it says

- `(hc : c ≠ ⊤)`: the constant $c \in [0, \infty]$ is finite.
- The conclusion: `HasFiniteMoment p (c • ν)`: the measure $c\nu$, given by $(c\nu)(A) = c \, \nu(A)$, has finite $p$-th moment.

The same base point serves. For $0 < p < \infty$, $\int d(x_0, y)^p \, d(c\nu)(y) = c \int d(x_0, y)^p \, d\nu(y) < \infty$; for $p = \infty$, the essential bound is unchanged when $c > 0$ and is $0$ when $c = 0$. The hypothesis $c \ne \infty$ is needed for $0 < p < \infty$: $\infty \cdot \nu$ has infinite moment unless the distance from the base point vanishes $\nu$-almost everywhere. Nothing is asked of the total mass of $\nu$.
