## What it says
For an element $m$ of a subcomodule $N$ of a right $C$-comodule $M$, the coaction $\rho(m)$ lies in the image of $N \otimes_R C$ in $M \otimes_R C$.

- `[CommSemiring R]`: the scalars $R$ form a commutative semiring.
- `[AddCommMonoid C] [Module R C] [Coalgebra R C]`: $C$ is an $R$-coalgebra, with comultiplication $\Delta : C \to C \otimes_R C$ and counit $\varepsilon : C \to R$.
- `[AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M] [Comodule R C M]`: $M$ is a right $C$-comodule, with an $R$-linear coaction $\rho : M \to M \otimes_R C$.
- `(N : Subcomodule R C M)`: a subcomodule $N$ of $M$.
- `(hm : m ∈ N)`: an element $m$ of $M$ that lies in $N$.
- The conclusion: `Comodule.coact m ∈ (TensorProduct.map N.carrier.subtype LinearMap.id).range`, that is, $\rho(m)$ lies in the image of the map $\iota \otimes \mathrm{id}_C : N \otimes_R C \to M \otimes_R C$, where $\iota$ is the inclusion of $N$ in $M$.

This is the defining condition of a subcomodule, made available as a statement about every subcomodule. Over a field, where $\iota \otimes \mathrm{id}_C$ is injective, it reads $\rho(N) \subseteq N \otimes C$, the usual definition.

- $m$ is an implicit argument: Lean reads it off the hypothesis `hm`.

## What it says
For a nonempty directed family of subcomodules $N_i$ of a right $C$-comodule $M$, the supremum of the family has as its elements exactly the union of the $N_i$.

- `[CommSemiring R]`: the scalars $R$ form a commutative semiring.
- `[AddCommMonoid C] [Module R C] [Coalgebra R C]`: $C$ is an $R$-coalgebra, with comultiplication $\Delta$ and counit $\varepsilon$.
- `[AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M] [Comodule R C M]`: $M$ is a right $C$-comodule, with an $R$-linear coaction $\rho : M \to M \otimes_R C$.
- `[Nonempty iota]`: the index type `iota` has at least one element.
- `(N : iota → Subcomodule R C M)`: a family of subcomodules $N_i$ of $M$, one for each $i$ in `iota`.
- `(hN : Directed (fun (x1 x2 : Subcomodule R C M) => x1 ≤ x2) N)`: the family is directed: for any $i$ and $j$ there is a $k$ with $N_i \le N_k$ and $N_j \le N_k$.
- The conclusion: `↑(⨆ (i : iota), N i) = ⋃ (i : iota), ↑(N i)`, that is, the set of elements of $\bigvee_i N_i$ equals $\bigcup_i N_i$.

This is the comodule version of the familiar fact for submodules. A directed union of subcomodules is again one: two elements lie in a common $N_k$, so their sum does too, and if $m \in N_i$ then $\rho(m)$ lies in the image of $N_i \otimes C$, hence in that of the union tensored with $C$. So the union is the least subcomodule containing every $N_i$.

The first is the statement element by element; the second shows that suprema of subcomodules are taken among submodules, where a directed supremum is a union.

- `↑` turns a subcomodule into the set of its elements, so the equation is one between subsets of $M$; `⨆` is the supremum among subcomodules and `⋃` the union of sets.
- `[Nonempty iota]` cannot be dropped: for an empty family the supremum is the least subcomodule $\{0\}$, while the union is empty.
- `iota` is an implicit type in the universe `u_1`; Lean reads it off `N`. The other square-bracket arguments are hypotheses carried as typeclasses, which Lean finds by itself.
- `@[simp]` lets Lean's simplifier rewrite with this equation automatically; it does not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
The inverse image $f^{-1}(B)$ of a subcomodule $B$ of $N$ under a morphism of comodules $f : M \to N$, as a subcomodule of $M$.

- `[CommRing R]`: the scalars $R$ form a commutative ring.
- `[AddCommMonoid C] [Module R C] [Coalgebra R C]`: $C$ is an $R$-coalgebra, with comultiplication $\Delta$ and counit $\varepsilon$.
- `[Module.Flat R C]`: $C$ is flat as an $R$-module: tensoring with $C$ preserves injective maps and kernels.
- `[AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M] [Comodule R C M]`: $M$ is a right $C$-comodule, with coaction $\rho_M : M \to M \otimes_R C$.
- `[AddCommMonoid N] [Module R N] [Comodule R C N]`: $N$ is a second right $C$-comodule, with coaction $\rho_N$.
- `(B : Subcomodule R C N)`: a subcomodule $B$ of $N$.
- `(f : Comodule.Hom R C M N)`: a morphism of right comodules, an $R$-linear map $f : M \to N$ compatible with the coactions.
- The value, of type `Subcomodule R C M`: the subcomodule of $M$ whose underlying submodule is $f^{-1}(B) = \{m \in M : f(m) \in B\}$, the preimage of $B$'s submodule under the linear map of $f$.

The preimage of a subcomodule under a comodule map is again a subcomodule, a standard fact over a field. Here $R$ is a commutative ring and $C$ is flat, which is what makes the closure condition hold: $f^{-1}(B)$ is the kernel of $M \to N/B$, and tensoring with a flat $C$ keeps that kernel description, so $\rho_M(m)$ lands in the image of $f^{-1}(B) \otimes_R C$ whenever $f(m) \in B$.

## What it says
For a morphism of comodules $f : M \to N$, the inverse image of the zero subcomodule of $N$ has as its underlying submodule the kernel of $f$.

- `[CommRing R]`: the scalars $R$ form a commutative ring.
- `[AddCommMonoid C] [Module R C] [Coalgebra R C]`: $C$ is an $R$-coalgebra, with comultiplication $\Delta$ and counit $\varepsilon$.
- `[Module.Flat R C]`: $C$ is flat as an $R$-module, the hypothesis under which inverse images of subcomodules are subcomodules.
- `[AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M] [Comodule R C M]`: $M$ is a right $C$-comodule, with coaction $\rho_M : M \to M \otimes_R C$.
- `[AddCommMonoid N] [Module R N] [Comodule R C N]`: $N$ is a second right $C$-comodule, with coaction $\rho_N$.
- `(f : Comodule.Hom R C M N)`: a morphism of right comodules, an $R$-linear map $f : M \to N$ compatible with the coactions.
- The conclusion: `(⊥.comap f).toSubmodule = f.ker`. On the left, the submodule underlying $f^{-1}(\bot)$, the inverse image under $f$ of the least subcomodule $\bot$ of $N$; on the right, the kernel $\ker f = \{m \in M : f(m) = 0\}$ of the linear map underlying $f$.

The least subcomodule is $\{0\}$, so this is the familiar identity $f^{-1}(0) = \ker f$, recorded at the level of underlying submodules.

## What it says
For a morphism of comodules $f : M \to N$ and a subcomodule $B$ of $N$, the submodule underlying the inverse image $f^{-1}(B)$ is the ordinary preimage of $B$'s submodule under the linear map $f$.

- `[CommRing R]`: the scalars $R$ form a commutative ring.
- `[AddCommMonoid C] [Module R C] [Coalgebra R C]`: $C$ is an $R$-coalgebra, with comultiplication $\Delta$ and counit $\varepsilon$.
- `[Module.Flat R C]`: $C$ is flat as an $R$-module, the hypothesis under which inverse images of subcomodules are subcomodules.
- `[AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M] [Comodule R C M]`: $M$ is a right $C$-comodule, with coaction $\rho_M : M \to M \otimes_R C$.
- `[AddCommMonoid N] [Module R N] [Comodule R C N]`: $N$ is a second right $C$-comodule, with coaction $\rho_N$.
- `(B : Subcomodule R C N)`: a subcomodule $B$ of $N$.
- `(f : Comodule.Hom R C M N)`: a morphism of right comodules, an $R$-linear map $f : M \to N$ compatible with the coactions.
- The conclusion: `(B.comap f).toSubmodule = Submodule.comap f.toLinearMap B.toSubmodule`. On the left, the submodule underlying the subcomodule $f^{-1}(B)$ of $M$; on the right, $\{m \in M : f(m) \in B\}$, the preimage of the submodule underlying $B$ under the linear map underlying $f$.

So the inverse image of a subcomodule is computed as for submodules; only the closure under the coaction, which flatness provides, is extra. This is how inverse images of subcomodules are understood over a field.

## What it says
The subcomodules of a right $C$-comodule $M$ that are finitely generated as $R$-modules form a directed family under inclusion: any two of them lie in a third.

- `[CommSemiring R]`: the scalars $R$ form a commutative semiring.
- `[AddCommMonoid C] [Module R C] [Coalgebra R C]`: $C$ is an $R$-coalgebra, with comultiplication $\Delta : C \to C \otimes_R C$ and counit $\varepsilon : C \to R$.
- `[AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M] [Comodule R C M]`: $M$ is a right $C$-comodule, with an $R$-linear coaction $\rho : M \to M \otimes_R C$.
- The conclusion: `DirectedOn (fun (x1 x2 : Subcomodule R C M) => x1 ≤ x2) finiteSubcomodules`. Here `finiteSubcomodules` is the set of subcomodules of $M$ that are finitely generated as $R$-modules, and the statement says that for any two members $N_1$ and $N_2$ of it there is a member $N_3$ with $N_1 \le N_3$ and $N_2 \le N_3$.

The witness is the join $N_1 + N_2$: a sum of two subcomodules is a subcomodule, and a sum of two finitely generated modules is finitely generated. This directedness is the first step towards writing a comodule as the directed union of its finitely generated subcomodules.

## What it says
Over a field $k$, a one-dimensional subcomodule $L$ of a right $C$-comodule $M$ lies in the weight space of exactly one group-like element $\chi$ of $C$: there is a unique group-like $\chi$ with $\rho(v) = v \otimes \chi$ for all $v \in L$.

- `[Field k]`: the scalars $k$ form a field.
- `[AddCommMonoid C] [Module k C] [Coalgebra k C]`: $C$ is a $k$-coalgebra, with comultiplication $\Delta : C \to C \otimes_k C$ and counit $\varepsilon : C \to k$.
- `[AddCommGroup M] [Module k M] [Comodule k C M]`: $M$ is a $k$-vector space with a right $C$-comodule structure, a coaction $\rho : M \to M \otimes_k C$.
- `(L : Subcomodule k C M)`: a subcomodule $L$ of $M$.
- `(hL : Module.finrank k ↥L.toSubmodule = 1)`: $L$ has dimension $1$ over $k$, so $L = kv$ for some $v \neq 0$.

## What it says
Let $R$ be a commutative ring containing $\mathbb{Q}$, $A$ a commutative $R$-algebra, $G$ a finite monoid acting on $A$ by ring endomorphisms, and $x = (x_i)_{i \in \iota}$ any family in $A$, finite or not. Then for every monomial $x^d$, its orbit sum $\sum_{g \in G} g \cdot x^d$ is a polynomial with coefficients in $R$ in the orbit sums $\sum_{g} g \cdot x^e$ of the monomials of total degree at most $|G|$.

- `[CommRing R] [Algebra ℚ R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring with an algebra structure over $\mathbb{Q}$, one in which every nonzero integer is invertible.
- `[CommRing A] [Algebra R A]`: $A$ is a commutative $R$-algebra.
- `[Fintype G]`: $G$ is finite, with its elements listed, so that sums over $G$ and its order $|G|$ make sense.
- `[Monoid G]`: $G$ is a monoid; it need not be a group.
- `[MulSemiringAction G A]`: $G$ acts on $A$, each element by a ring endomorphism.
- `(x : ι → A)`: a family of elements $x_i$ of $A$, indexed by a type $\iota$.
- `(d : ι →₀ ℕ)`: an exponent vector, with finitely many nonzero entries, naming the monomial $x^d = \prod_i x_i^{d_i}$.
- The conclusion: the orbit sum $\sum_{g} g \cdot x^d$ lies in the subalgebra `Algebra.adjoin R` generated over $R$ by the image `''` of the set of exponent vectors $e$ with total degree `Finsupp.degree e` at most `Fintype.card G` $= |G|$, under the map $e \mapsto \sum_g g \cdot x^e$.

This is the key step of Noether's proof of her degree bound: the orbit sums are multisymmetric power sums in the $|G|$ vectors $(g \cdot x_i)_i$, and over $\mathbb{Q}$ Newton's identities express every power sum through those of degree at most $|G|$. The identity is purely polynomial, so it needs neither invertibility nor $R$-linearity of the action. For the swap of $x$ and $y$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x,y]$, it gives $x^3 + y^3$ from $x + y$, $x^2 + y^2$ and $2xy$.

## Lean subtleties
- No hypothesis says that the action commutes with the scalars of $R$: the coefficients used are rational, and every action by ring endomorphisms fixes them.
- `d.prod fun i n => x i ^ n` is the monomial $x^d$, a finite product even when $\iota$ is infinite.
- The orbit sums are not divided by $|G|$.
- For $d = 0$ the orbit sum is $|G| \cdot 1$, itself one of the generators, of degree $0$.
- `[Algebra ℚ R]` cannot be dropped: over $\mathbb{F}_2$, with the swap in $\mathbb{F}_2[x,y]$, the orbit sums of degree at most $2$ generate $\mathbb{F}_2[x+y]$, which misses the orbit sum $x^2y + xy^2 = xy(x+y)$.

## What it says
For a quadratic form $Q$ on a free module $M$ with an orthogonal basis $b$ whose vectors satisfy $Q(b_i) = \pm 1$, the Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(Q)$ is the group algebra $R[\Gamma]$ of the group $\Gamma$ of signed monomials, modulo the ideal generated by $\varepsilon + 1$, where $\varepsilon$ is the element $-1$ of $\Gamma$.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring.
- `[AddCommGroup M] [Module R M]`: $M$ is an $R$-module, carrying the quadratic form $Q$ and the basis $b = (b_i)_{i \in I}$, both implicit.
- `[Invertible 2]`: $2$ is invertible in $R$.
- `[LinearOrder I]`: the index set $I$ of the basis is linearly ordered.
- `(hb : LinearMap.IsOrthoᵢ (QuadraticMap.associated Q) ⇑b)`: the basis is orthogonal for the symmetric bilinear form $B(u,v) = \frac12\bigl(Q(u+v) - Q(u) - Q(v)\bigr)$ of $Q$: $B(b_i, b_j) = 0$ for $i \ne j$.
- `(hQ : ∀ (i : I), Q (b i) = 1 ∨ Q (b i) = -1)`: each basis vector has $Q(b_i) = 1$ or $Q(b_i) = -1$.
- The type: an isomorphism of $R$-algebras `≃ₐ[R]` from the quotient `⧸` of `MonoidAlgebra R ↥(monomialGroup Q ⇑b)`, the group algebra $R[\Gamma]$ of the subgroup $\Gamma$ of units of $\mathrm{Cl}(Q)$ generated by $-1$ and the $b_i$, by `Ideal.span` of the element $[\varepsilon] + 1$, to `CliffordAlgebra Q`.

Its value: the ideal is identified with the kernel of the algebra map $R[\Gamma] \to \mathrm{Cl}(Q)$ sending each group element to its value, which is onto, and the first isomorphism theorem gives the rest. So the class of $\gamma \in \Gamma$ goes to $\gamma$ itself, as the docstring says. This is the standard presentation of a Clifford algebra with an orthonormal-type basis as a twisted group algebra, here over any commutative ring in which $2$ is invertible and for a basis of any size.

## Lean subtleties
- Mathlib's Clifford algebra imposes $v^2 = Q(v)$. For the opposite sign convention, apply the statement to $-Q$, which `hQ` allows as well.
- `Ideal.span` in the noncommutative ring $R[\Gamma]$ is the left ideal generated by the element; since $\varepsilon$ is central, it is two-sided, and the quotient is the algebra $R[\Gamma]/(\varepsilon + 1)$, in which $[\varepsilon\gamma] = -[\gamma]$.
- `[Invertible 2]` is a hypothesis carried as a typeclass; it is what makes the bilinear form `QuadraticMap.associated Q` defined.
- `[LinearOrder I]` restricts nothing, since every index set can be ordered, and the map does not depend on the order.
- `⇑b` is the basis viewed as the function $i \mapsto b_i$. The index set may be infinite, and then so is $\Gamma$.
- The zero ring is allowed, since $2$ is invertible there; both sides are then $0$.

## What it says
For a quadratic form $Q$ on a free module $M$ with an orthogonal basis $b$ whose vectors satisfy $Q(b_i) = \pm 1$, and for any $R$-algebra $A$, the $R$-algebra maps $\mathrm{Cl}(Q) \to A$ correspond one-to-one to the monoid maps $f : \Gamma \to A$ from the group $\Gamma$ of signed monomials with $f(\varepsilon) = -1$, where $\varepsilon$ is the element $-1$ of $\Gamma$.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring.
- `[AddCommGroup M] [Module R M]`: $M$ is an $R$-module, carrying the quadratic form $Q$ and the basis $b = (b_i)_{i \in I}$, both implicit.
- `[Invertible 2]`: $2$ is invertible in $R$.
- `[LinearOrder I]`: the index set $I$ of the basis is linearly ordered.
- `(hb : LinearMap.IsOrthoᵢ (QuadraticMap.associated Q) ⇑b)`: the basis is orthogonal for the symmetric bilinear form $B(u,v) = \frac12\bigl(Q(u+v) - Q(u) - Q(v)\bigr)$ of $Q$: $B(b_i, b_j) = 0$ for $i \ne j$.
- `(hQ : ∀ (i : I), Q (b i) = 1 ∨ Q (b i) = -1)`: each basis vector has $Q(b_i) = 1$ or $Q(b_i) = -1$.
- `[Ring A] [Algebra R A]`: $A$ is an $R$-algebra, not necessarily commutative.
- The type: a bijection `≃` between the set of monoid maps `↥(monomialGroup Q ⇑b) →* A` sending `monomialGroupEpsilon Q ⇑b`, that is $\varepsilon$, to $-1$, and the set of $R$-algebra maps `CliffordAlgebra Q →ₐ[R] A`. Here $\Gamma$ is the subgroup of units of $\mathrm{Cl}(Q)$ generated by $-1$ and the $b_i$.

Its value: an algebra map $F$ goes to its restriction $\gamma \mapsto F(\gamma)$ to $\Gamma$; a monoid map $f$ goes to the algebra map that extends it, which exists because $f(b_i)^2 = Q(b_i)$ and $f(b_i) f(b_j) = -f(b_j) f(b_i)$ for $i \ne j$ follow from $f(\varepsilon) = -1$. This is the universal property of the Clifford algebra, rewritten for the generators $b_i$; for $A$ the endomorphisms of a module $W$ it identifies Clifford module structures on $W$ with representations of $\Gamma$ in which $\varepsilon$ acts by $-1$, as the docstring says.

## What it says
If a module $V$ is the internal direct sum of submodules $A_i$, and a submodule $p$ contains the $i$-th component of each of its elements for every $i$, then $p$ is the sum of its intersections with the summands: $\sum_i (p \cap A_i) = p$.

- `[Semiring S]`: $S$ is a semiring, not necessarily commutative, and not necessarily with negatives.
- `[AddCommMonoid V] [Module S V]`: $V$ is a module over $S$, with a family $A = (A_i)_{i \in \kappa}$ of submodules, implicit.
- `[DecidableEq κ]`: equality of indices in $\kappa$ can be decided, which the construction of the direct sum uses.
- `(h : IsInternal A)`: the canonical map $\bigoplus_i A_i \to V$, adding up the components, is bijective, so every $v \in V$ is uniquely a finite sum $\sum_i v_i$ with $v_i \in A_i$.
- `(p : Submodule S V)`: a submodule $p$ of $V$.
- `(hp : ∀ m ∈ p, ∀ (i : κ), ↑(((LinearEquiv.ofBijective (coeLinearMap A) h).symm m) i) ∈ p)`: for every $m \in p$ and every index $i$, the component $m_i \in A_i$ of $m$, read off through the inverse of that bijection and viewed in $V$, lies in $p$.
- The conclusion: `⨆ (i : κ), p ⊓ A i = p`, the submodule generated by the intersections $p \cap A_i$ is $p$.

This is the standard criterion for a submodule of a graded module to be graded, in its spanning form, here for any internal direct sum decomposition of a module over a semiring and any index set.

The test applies the statement where $p$ is a weight space, which contains the components of its elements, and recovers the expected additivity of dimensions.

## Lean subtleties
- `⨆` is the supremum of submodules, the submodule of finite sums of their elements; `⊓` is intersection.
- The conclusion states only that the $p \cap A_i$ span $p$; the sum is direct as well, since the $A_i$ are independent.
- The index set may be infinite: each element has only finitely many nonzero components.
- When $\kappa$ is empty, `IsInternal A` forces $V = 0$, and both sides are $0$.
- `[DecidableEq κ]` is a typeclass that restricts nothing mathematically.

## What it says
The Cartan, or polar, decomposition of the general linear group over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$: the map $(k, X) \mapsto k \exp X$ is a homeomorphism from the product of the unitary group and the space of Hermitian matrices onto the group of invertible matrices.

- `(n : Type u_1) (𝕜 : Type u_2)`: the type n indexing the rows and columns of the matrices, and the scalars 𝕜.
- `[RCLike 𝕜]`: 𝕜 is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
- `[Fintype n] [DecidableEq n]`: n is finite, with decidable equality, so the matrices are square of size $|n|$.
- The type: a homeomorphism `≃ₜ` from `↥(unitaryGroup n 𝕜) × ↥(selfAdjoint (Matrix n n 𝕜))`, the pairs $(k, X)$ of a unitary matrix $k$ ($k^* k = 1$) and a self-adjoint matrix $X$ ($X^* = X$), to `GL n 𝕜`, the group of invertible matrices.

Its value: the forward map is $(k, X) \mapsto k \exp X$, with $\exp$ the matrix exponential; it is the general Cartan decomposition of the units of a complete normed $\mathbb{R}$-algebra with a continuous functional calculus, applied to the matrix algebra with the $\ell^2$ operator norm. Its inverse sends $g$ to its polar decomposition: $g = k p$ with $k$ unitary and $p = (g^* g)^{1/2}$ positive definite, and $X = \log p$.

For 𝕜 $= \mathbb{R}$ this is $O(n) \times \mathrm{Sym}(n) \cong GL(n, \mathbb{R})$, and for 𝕜 $= \mathbb{C}$ it is $U(n) \times \mathrm{Herm}(n) \cong GL(n, \mathbb{C})$: the standard polar decomposition, as a homeomorphism.

## Lean subtleties
- Over $\mathbb{R}$ the unitary group is the orthogonal group and the self-adjoint matrices are the symmetric ones, since the star operation is the transpose there.
- The $\ell^2$ operator norm is used only inside the construction. The topologies in the statement are the usual ones on matrices, and on `GL n 𝕜` that of the units, in which a matrix and its inverse vary continuously.
- `≃ₜ` is only a homeomorphism: it is not a group isomorphism, and the self-adjoint matrices form an additive group, not a multiplicative one.
- When n is empty, all three spaces are a single point.

## What it says
Every invertible real $n \times n$ matrix $g$ factors uniquely as $g = k a u$, with $k$ orthogonal, $a$ diagonal with positive diagonal entries, and $u$ upper unitriangular: the Iwasawa decomposition $G = KAN$ of $GL_n(\mathbb{R})$.

- `(g : GL (Fin n) ℝ)`: an invertible real matrix $g$ of size $n$, its rows and columns indexed by $0, \dots, n-1$; the size $n$ is implicit.
- The conclusion: there is exactly one triple `x` $= (k, a, u)$ in the product of `unitarySubgroup (GL (Fin n) ℝ)`, the matrices with $k^{\mathsf T} k = k k^{\mathsf T} = 1$, `posDiagonalSubgroup (Fin n) ℝ`, the diagonal matrices with positive diagonal entries, and `upperUnitriangularGroup (Fin n) ℝ`, the upper triangular matrices with $1$s on the diagonal, such that $k \cdot a \cdot u = g$.

This is the standard Iwasawa decomposition of the general linear group, in the order $K \cdot A \cdot N$. In matrix terms it is the QR factorisation $g = k r$ from Gram–Schmidt applied to the columns of $g$, with $r = a u$ upper triangular with positive diagonal, split into its diagonal $a$ and the unitriangular $u = a^{-1} r$.

- "Upper" refers to the natural order of `Fin n`: the entries below the diagonal vanish.
- `∃!` asserts existence and uniqueness of the whole triple; the `↑` are the inclusions of the three subgroups into `GL (Fin n) ℝ`.
- For $n = 0$ all the groups are trivial, and the statement holds with the empty matrix.

## What it says
The mesh property of the Auslander–Reiten quiver of a finite-dimensional algebra $A$ over a field $k$: if the Auslander–Reiten translate of the vertex $m$ is $t = \tau m$, then for every vertex $x$ there are as many arrows $x \to m$ as arrows $t \to x$.

- `(k : Type u) (A : Type v)`: the field k and the algebra A.
- `[Field k]`: k is a field, not necessarily algebraically closed.
- `[Ring A] [Algebra k A] [FiniteDimensional k A]`: A is a finite-dimensional algebra over k, not necessarily commutative.
- `(h : (arTranslation k A).translate m = some t)`: the vertex m, an isomorphism class of indecomposable finitely generated A-modules, is not projective, and its Auslander–Reiten translate $\tau m$ is the vertex t; both m and t are implicit.
- `(x : TauCeti.IrreducibleMorphismQuiver k fun (M : ModuleCat A) => Module.Finite A ↑M)`: any vertex x of the quiver whose vertices are the isomorphism classes of indecomposable finitely generated A-modules, and whose arrows record the irreducible maps between them.
- The conclusion: `Nat.card (x ⟶ m) = Nat.card (t ⟶ x)`, the number of arrows from x to m equals the number of arrows from t to x.

This is the standard mesh relation: both counts are read off the almost split sequence $0 \to \tau m \to E \to m \to 0$, in whose middle term $E$ the module $x$ occurs as often as there are irreducible maps $x \to m$, and as there are irreducible maps $\tau m \to x$, counted with the same multiplicity.

- `Module.Finite A ↑M` restricts the vertices to finitely generated modules, the setting of Auslander–Reiten theory.

## What it says
If $\chi : G \to M$ is a homomorphism from a group into a commutative monoid, then for any function $f : M \to k$ the function $g \mapsto f(\chi(g))$ on $G$ is a class function: it is constant on conjugacy classes.

- `[Semiring k]`: $k$ is a semiring, in which the functions take their values.
- `[Group G]`: $G$ is a group, not necessarily finite.
- `[CommMonoid M]`: $M$ is a commutative monoid.
- `(χ : G →* M)`: a monoid homomorphism χ from $G$ to $M$.
- `(f : M → k)`: an arbitrary function f from $M$ to $k$, with no condition on it.
- The conclusion: the function $g \mapsto f(\chi(g))$ belongs to `TauCeti.ClassFunction k G`, the $k$-submodule of the functions $G \to k$ that are constant under conjugation.

The reason is that conjugation is invisible in a commutative target: $\chi(hgh^{-1}) = \chi(h)\chi(g)\chi(h^{-1}) = \chi(g)\chi(hh^{-1}) = \chi(g)$. The docstring's example is a linear character $\chi : G \to k^\times$, read in $k$: this is the standard fact that one-dimensional characters, and anything computed from their values, are class functions.

## Lean subtleties
- `G →* M` is a map of monoids: it is multiplicative and sends $1$ to $1$. Since $G$ is a group, each $\chi(h)$ is invertible in $M$, with inverse $\chi(h^{-1})$.
- The outer function f need not preserve addition, multiplication or scalars, so the class function obtained need not be a character.
- `ClassFunction k G` is defined for any group, finite or not; nothing here requires $G$ to be finite or $k$ to be a field.
- When $M$ is the trivial monoid, the function is constant, and constant functions are class functions.

## What it says
An irreducible, reduced, crystallographic root system over $\mathbb{Q}$ with finitely many roots is isomorphic to the model root system of a Dynkin type $t$ exactly when $t$ is the Dynkin type read off from a base: it is isomorphic to the model of its own type and to no other, and the type does not depend on the base chosen.

- `[AddCommGroup M] [Module ℚ M]`: $M$ is a vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$, the space of the roots.
- `[AddCommGroup N] [Module ℚ N]`: $N$ is a vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$, the space of the coroots. The root pairing $P$ on $M$ and $N$, with roots and coroots indexed by $\iota$, is implicit.
- `[Finite ι]`: there are finitely many roots.
- `[Nonempty ι]`: there is at least one root.
- `[P.IsRootSystem]`: the roots span $M$ and the coroots span $N$.
- `[P.IsCrystallographic]`: every pairing of a root with a coroot is an integer.
- `[P.IsReduced]`: two linearly dependent roots differ at most by a sign.
- `[P.IsIrreducible]`: $P$ is nontrivial and has no proper invariant subspace.
- `(b : P.Base)`: a base b of $P$, a set of simple roots.
- `(ht : t.Valid)`: the Dynkin type $t$, implicit, lies in the rank ranges on which the types are pairwise distinct and irreducible.
- The conclusion: there is an isomorphism `P.Equiv (t.rationalRootSystem ht)` from $P$ to the model root system of type $t$, which lives in $\mathbb{Q}^{\mathrm{rank}\, t}$, if and only if $t$ equals `TauCeti.classifiedDynkinType b`, the type of the Cartan matrix of b.

This is the classification of irreducible reduced root systems in the form "each is isomorphic to exactly one model", with the standard facts that the type is an isomorphism invariant, independent of the base since the Weyl group permutes the bases transitively.

## What it says
The open fundamental alcove of a base $b$ of a finite root system: the set of points $x$ of the coweight space at which every simple root is positive and the highest root $\theta$ is less than $1$.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring, the scalars.
- `[AddCommGroup M] [Module R M]`: $M$ is an $R$-module, the space of the roots.
- `[AddCommGroup N] [Module R N]`: $N$ is an $R$-module, the space of the coroots, the coweight space.
- `(P : RootPairing ι R M N)`: a root pairing P, with roots in $M$ and coroots in $N$ indexed by $\iota$, and $M$ and $N$ perfectly paired.
- `(b : P.Base)`: a base b of P, a set of simple roots.
- `[CharZero R]`: $R$ has characteristic zero.
- `[Finite ι] [Nonempty ι]`: there are finitely many roots, and at least one.
- `[Preorder R]`: an order on $R$, used for the inequalities.

Its value: the set of $x \in N$ with $\alpha_i(x) > 0$ for every simple root $\alpha_i$ of b, and $\theta(x) < 1$, where `P.root' i` is the root $\alpha_i$ read as a linear form on $N$, and $\theta$ is `b.highestRoot`, a root of maximal height relative to b.

For a reduced irreducible root system over $\mathbb{R}$ this is the standard open fundamental alcove $\{x : \langle \alpha_i, x\rangle > 0 \text{ for all } i,\ \langle \theta, x\rangle < 1\}$, a cell of the arrangement of the affine hyperplanes $\{x : \alpha(x) = k\}$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, on which the affine Weyl group acts.

## Lean subtleties
- `b.highestRoot` is only a root of maximal height. When P is reduced and irreducible it is the highest root $\theta$, unique, as the docstring says; for a reducible system one such root is picked, and the set is not the classical alcove, which is then a product of the alcoves of the components.
- `[Preorder R]` is separate from the ring structure: no compatibility of the order with addition or multiplication is assumed. For $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{Q}$ it is the usual order.
- The alcove lives in the coweight space $N$, where the roots act as linear forms; it is open, the inequalities being strict.
- In rank one, with simple root $\alpha = \theta$, it is the interval $\{x : 0 < \alpha(x) < 1\}$.

## What it says
The carrier of the Cayley–Dickson double of $A$: the ordered pairs $(a, b)$ of elements of $A$.

- `(A : Type u_1)`: any type A; the ring operations and the involution $a \mapsto a^*$ that the doubling uses are supplied separately, for the A that have them.

Its fields:

- `fst : A`: the first coordinate $a$.
- `snd : A`: the second coordinate $b$.

The docstring records the multiplication that the double carries, defined apart from this structure: $(a, b)(c, d) = (ac - d^* b,\ da + b c^*)$. With it, doubling the real numbers, the complex numbers and the quaternions gives the complex numbers, the quaternions and the octonions: this is the standard Cayley–Dickson construction, and the structure is its underlying set $A \times A$.

## What it says
A function on the conjugacy classes of $G$ gives a class function on $G$: the function $g \mapsto f([g])$, where $[g]$ is the conjugacy class of $g$.

- `[Semiring k]`: $k$ is a semiring, in which the functions take their values.

Its value is $g \mapsto f([g])$, composing $f$ with the quotient map $g \mapsto [g]$ (`ConjClasses.mk`), together with the proof that it is constant on classes: $h g h^{-1}$ and $g$ are conjugate, so they have the same class and the same value.

This is the standard way a function on conjugacy classes is read as a class function, the inverse of evaluating a class function on classes. No representative of a class is chosen: the class of each element is used directly.

For a finite group $G$ and a class function $f$, the sum of $f$ over $G$ is the sum over the conjugacy classes $C$ of $|C|$ times the value of $f$ on $C$:
$$\sum_{g \in G} f(g) = \sum_{C} |C| \, f(C).$$

- `[Semiring k]`: $k$ is a semiring, in which the class function takes its values.
- `[Group G]`: $G$ is a group.
- `[Fintype G]`: $G$ is finite, with its finitely many elements available to sum over.
- `[Fintype (ConjClasses G)]`: the set of conjugacy classes of $G$ is finite, with its elements available to sum over; for a finite group this is automatic.
- `(f : ↥(ClassFunction k G))`: a class function $f$ on $G$, a function $G \to k$ constant on conjugacy classes.
- The conclusion: the sum of $f(g)$ over all $g \in G$ equals the sum over all conjugacy classes $C$ of `Nat.card ↑C.carrier`, the number of elements of $C$, read as an element of $k$, times `toConjClasses f C`, the common value of $f$ on $C$.

This is the usual regrouping of a sum over a finite group by conjugacy classes, which, as the docstring says, turns sums over the group into sums over the columns of a character table, each column weighted by its class size. No division by $|G|$ occurs, so the formula holds over any semiring.

## What it says
For a Hopf algebra $H$ over a commutative ring $R$, `centralAugmentation R H` is the set of the central elements of $H$ that the counit sends to $0$, the intersection $Z(H) \cap \ker \varepsilon$, as an $R$-submodule of $H$.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$, any type, is a commutative ring, the ring of scalars.
- `[Ring H] [HopfAlgebra R H]`: $H$ is a ring with the structure of a Hopf algebra over $R$: an $R$-algebra with a comultiplication, a counit $\varepsilon \colon H \to R$ and an antipode satisfying the usual axioms.
- The result: an $R$-submodule of $H$ (`Submodule R H`).

Its value is `(Subalgebra.center R H).toSubmodule ⊓ (augmentation R H).toIdeal.restrictScalars R`: the meet, that is the intersection, of two $R$-submodules of $H$. The first is the center $Z(H)$, the elements that commute with every element of $H$, seen as an $R$-submodule. The second is the augmentation ideal, the kernel of the counit $\varepsilon$, a two-sided ideal of $H$, seen as an $R$-submodule by restricting its scalars from $H$ to $R$.

This is the central part of the augmentation ideal, as the docstring says. It is closed under addition, under multiplication by scalars of $R$ and under products, but in general not under multiplication by arbitrary elements of $H$, which is why it is a submodule and not an ideal.

This is the ideal generated by the central part of the augmentation ideal, as the docstring says.

This is the defining property of the ideal generated by a set: it is the smallest ideal containing the set, so it lies in an ideal exactly when the set does. The statement holds for every ideal $I$, not only two-sided ones.

## What it says
The path algebra $kQ$ of a quiver $Q$ over $k$, as a type: the finite $k$-linear combinations of the paths of $Q$. Its product, concatenation of composable paths with the later factor written first and $0$ on pairs that do not meet, is put on this type separately.

- `[Zero k]`: the coefficients `k` need only have a $0$ for the type to be formed; the operations on it ask more of `k`.
- `[Quiver Q]`: `Q` is the set of vertices of a quiver, a directed graph that may have loops and several arrows between two vertices.

Its value is `Quiver.TotalPath Q →₀ k`: the functions from the paths of $Q$, each with its source and target, to $k$ that are $0$ at all but finitely many paths. A path $x$ with coefficient $c$ is the function that is $c$ at $x$ and $0$ elsewhere, so the paths form a basis.

This is the path algebra as the literature defines it: its basis is the set of paths, the trivial path at each vertex included, and the product of two paths is their concatenation when they meet and $0$ otherwise. The order is that of composition of maps, $xy$ tracing $y$ and then $x$.

- `TauCeti.PathAlgebra.single_mul_single` — the product of two basis paths is their concatenation, later factor first, when they meet, and $0$ otherwise.

- `TauCeti.Quiver.Kronecker.finrank_pathAlgebra_eq_three` — the path algebra of $A_2$, two vertices and one arrow, has dimension $3$.

All five pass. The first two pin down the product and the unit; the dimension counts show that the basis is the set of all paths, trivial ones included, and that a loop gives infinitely many.

## What it says
The paths of a quiver $Q$ form a basis of its path algebra $kQ$ over $k$: the basis vector of a path $x$ is $x$ itself, with coefficient $1$.

- `[Semiring k]`: the coefficients `k` form a semiring, with a $0$ and a $1$; a ring or a field is a special case.
- `[Quiver Q]`: `Q` is the set of vertices of a quiver, a directed graph that may have loops and several arrows between two vertices.

Its value is `Finsupp.basisSingleOne`: the basis of the finitely supported functions from the paths to $k$, `pathAlgebra k Q`, whose vector at a path $x$ is the function that is $1$ at $x$ and $0$ elsewhere. It is indexed by `Quiver.TotalPath Q`, the paths with their sources and targets, trivial paths at the vertices included, and the coordinates of an element are its coefficients on the paths.

This is the basis the path algebra is defined by in the literature: its elements are the finite linear combinations of paths, and each has one way of being written so. No finiteness of the quiver is assumed.

## What it says
For a complex class function $f$ on the symmetric group $S_n$, the coefficient of the Schur polynomial $s_\mu$ in its Frobenius characteristic, in $d \geq n$ variables, is the pairing $\langle \chi^\mu, f \rangle$ of $f$ with the character of the Specht module of $\mu$.

- `(d : ℕ)`: a natural number $d$, the number of variables.
- `(h : n ≤ d)`: there are at least as many variables as the degree $n$.
- `(f : ↥(ClassFunction ℂ (Equiv.Perm (Fin n))))`: a class function $f$ on $S_n$, the permutations of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$: a function to $\mathbb{C}$ that is constant on conjugacy classes.
- `(μ : { ν : n.Partition // ν.parts.card ≤ Fintype.card (Fin d) })`: a partition $\mu$ of $n$ with at most $d$ parts, the partitions that index the Schur basis in $d$ variables; since $d \geq n$, every partition of $n$ is one.
- The conclusion: the $\mu$-coordinate, in `schurPolyBasis (Fin d) ℂ n`, the basis of Schur polynomials of the symmetric polynomials of degree $n$, of `frobeniusCharacteristic n d h f`, the Frobenius characteristic of $f$, equals `ClassFunction.characterPairing` of the character of `spechtModuleℂ ↑μ`, the complex Specht module $S^\mu$, with $f$.

This is the classical expansion $\mathrm{ch}(f) = \sum_\mu \langle \chi^\mu, f \rangle\, s_\mu$, read one Schur coefficient at a time: the Specht characters are an orthonormal basis of the class functions, $\langle \chi^\mu, f \rangle$ is the $\chi^\mu$-coordinate of $f$, and the characteristic sends $\chi^\mu$ to $s_\mu$.

## What it says
The Cauchy identity in degree $n$: for finite families $x = (x_i)_{i \in σ}$ and $y = (y_j)_{j \in τ}$ in a commutative semiring, $\sum_{\lambda \vdash n} s_\lambda(x)\, s_\lambda(y) = h_n(x_i y_j)$, the complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial of degree $n$ evaluated at all the products $x_i y_j$.

- `[Fintype σ] [DecidableEq σ]`: the alphabet $σ$ is finite, and its letters can be compared for equality.
- `[Fintype τ] [DecidableEq τ]`: the same for a second alphabet $τ$.
- `[CommSemiring R] [CommSemiring S] [Algebra R S]`: $R$ and $S$ are commutative semirings, and $S$ is an algebra over $R$; the Schur polynomials are taken with coefficients in $R$ and evaluated in $S$.
- `(f : σ → S)`: a family $x_i = f(i)$ of elements of $S$, one for each letter of $σ$.
- `(g : τ → S)`: a family $y_j = g(j)$ of elements of $S$, one for each letter of $τ$.
- `(n : ℕ)`: a natural number $n$, the degree.
- The conclusion: the sum over all partitions $\mu$ of $n$ of `schurPoly σ R μ` evaluated at $f$ times `schurPoly τ R μ` evaluated at $g$ equals `MvPolynomial.hsymm (σ × τ) R n`, the complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial $h_n$ in variables indexed by the pairs $(i, j)$, evaluated at $x_i y_j$.

This is the coefficient of $t^n$ in the Cauchy identity $\sum_\lambda s_\lambda(x) s_\lambda(y) = \prod_{i,j} (1 - x_i y_j)^{-1}$, since $\prod_{i,j} (1 - x_i y_j t)^{-1} = \sum_n h_n(x_i y_j)\, t^n$. Stated degree by degree, it needs no power series, and it holds over any commutative semiring.

## What it says
The inverse of Frobenius's formula: for a partition $\mu$ of $n$, $\sum_{\pi \in S_n} \chi^\mu(\pi)\, p_{\rho(\pi)} = n!\, s_\mu$, where $\chi^\mu$ is the character of the Specht module $S^\mu$, $\rho(\pi)$ the cycle type of $\pi$, and $p_\rho$ the product of the power sums $p_{\rho_i}$; in any finite set of variables and over any commutative ring.

- `[Fintype σ]`: the alphabet $σ$, the set of variables, is finite.
- `[CommRing R]`: the coefficients `R` form a commutative ring with a $1$.
- `(μ : n.Partition)`: a partition $\mu$ of $n$, a finite multiset of positive integers with sum $n$.
- The conclusion: the sum over all permutations $\pi$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ of `spechtChar μ π`, the integer $\chi^\mu(\pi)$, times `MvPolynomial.psumPart σ R π.partition`, the product $p_{\rho(\pi)} = \prod_i p_{\rho_i}$ of the power sums $p_k = \sum_{x \in σ} x^k$ over the parts of the cycle type of $\pi$, equals $n!$ times `schurPoly σ R μ`, the Schur polynomial $s_\mu$ in the variables $σ$.

Grouping the permutations by cycle type, $n!/z_\rho$ of them having type $\rho$, this is the classical $s_\mu = \sum_\rho z_\rho^{-1} \chi^\mu(\rho)\, p_\rho$, which expresses the Schur functions through the power sums. It is multiplied through by $n!$, so it holds where $n!$ cannot be inverted; over a ring containing $\mathbb{Q}$ it says that $\frac{1}{n!} \sum_\pi \chi^\mu(\pi)\, p_{\rho(\pi)} = s_\mu$.

## What it says
A seminormed ring that has a multiplicative pseudo-uniformiser gives its identity the norm $1$.

- `[SeminormedRing R]`: a ring $R$ with a real-valued seminorm $\|\cdot\|$ that is submultiplicative, $\|xy\| \le \|x\|\,\|y\|$. Nothing in `SeminormedRing` asks that $\|1\| = 1$.
- `(ϖ : PseudoUniformizer R)`: a multiplicative pseudo-uniformiser ϖ of $R$: a unit with $0 < \|\varpi\| < 1$ by which left multiplication scales the norm exactly, $\|\varpi x\| = \|\varpi\|\,\|x\|$ for every $x \in R$.
- The conclusion: `‖1‖ = 1`, the norm of the identity of $R$ is the real number $1$.

It is the case $x = 1$ of the scaling: $\|\varpi\| = \|\varpi\|\,\|1\|$, and $\|\varpi\| > 0$ can be cancelled. Where a source takes $\|1\| = 1$ as part of its standing setting, this lemma shows that a multiplicative pseudo-uniformiser already gives it, so it need not be assumed separately.

## References and tests
- [JN §2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1604.07739#page=8) — seminormed rings with a multiplicative pseudo-uniformiser, the setting of this lemma.
- `TauCeti.NormedRing.PseudoUniformizer.norm_inv` — passes: the inverse of the unit ϖ has the reciprocal norm, $\|\varpi^{-1}\| = \|\varpi\|^{-1}$.
- `TauCeti.NormedRing.PseudoUniformizer.nontrivial` — passes: a ring with a pseudo-uniformiser is not the zero ring.

The zero ring, where $1 = 0$ and so $\|1\| = 0$, is the obvious threat to the statement, and the second test shows that it has no pseudo-uniformiser. The first is the companion identity $\|\varpi\|\,\|\varpi^{-1}\| = \|\varpi \varpi^{-1}\| = \|1\| = 1$, which rests on this lemma.

## What it says
If some element $u$ has nonzero norm and multiplying by it on the left scales every norm by $\|u\|$, then $\|1\| = 1$.

- `[MulOneClass R]`: $R$ has a multiplication and an element $1$ with $1 \cdot a = a = a \cdot 1$ for all $a$; no associativity and no addition are asked for.
- `[Norm R]`: a function $\|\cdot\| : R \to \mathbb{R}$, with no axioms at all: not a seminorm, not even nonnegative.
- `(hu0 : ‖u‖ ≠ 0)`: the element $u \in R$ has nonzero norm.
- `(hu : ∀ (x : R), ‖u * x‖ = ‖u‖ * ‖x‖)`: left multiplication by $u$ scales norms exactly, $\|ux\| = \|u\|\,\|x\|$ for every $x \in R$.
- The conclusion: `‖1‖ = 1`, the norm of the identity of $R$ is the real number $1$.

It is the case $x = 1$ of `hu`: $\|u\| = \|u \cdot 1\| = \|u\|\,\|1\|$, and $\|u\| \neq 0$ cancels. In a normed ring this is the familiar remark that an element on which the norm is multiplicative forces $\|1\| = 1$; here the remark is stated with only the algebra it uses.

## What it says
For a unit $u$ of a monoid that has nonzero norm and by which left multiplication scales every norm by $\|u\|$, the inverse has the reciprocal norm, $\|u^{-1}\| = \|u\|^{-1}$.

- `[Monoid R]`: $R$ is a monoid: an associative multiplication with an identity $1$.
- `[Norm R]`: a function $\|\cdot\| : R \to \mathbb{R}$, with no axioms at all.
- `(hu0 : ‖↑u‖ ≠ 0)`: the unit $u$ of $R$, an invertible element given by the implicit `{u : Rˣ}`, has nonzero norm.
- `(hu : ∀ (x : R), ‖↑u * x‖ = ‖↑u‖ * ‖x‖)`: left multiplication by $u$ scales norms exactly: $\|ux\| = \|u\|\,\|x\|$ for every $x \in R$.
- The conclusion: `‖↑u⁻¹‖ = ‖↑u‖⁻¹`, the inverse of $u$, viewed in $R$, has norm the reciprocal of $\|u\|$.

From `hu` at $x = 1$ and at $x = u^{-1}$: $\|u\| = \|u\|\,\|1\|$ and $\|1\| = \|u\|\,\|u^{-1}\|$, and $\|u\| \neq 0$ gives first $\|1\| = 1$ and then $\|u^{-1}\| = \|u\|^{-1}$. This is the forward direction of the usual characterisation of multiplicative units of a seminormed ring with $\|1\| = 1$, stated without addition, without the inequalities of a norm, which it does not use, and without assuming $\|1\| = 1$, which follows.

## What it says
On a Riemannian manifold whose curvature has, near a point $x$, the pointwise constant-curvature form with a function $\kappa$ differentiable at $x$, the covariant derivative of the curvature at $x$ is $d\kappa$ times that same algebraic form.

- `[NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`: $E$ is a finite-dimensional real normed space, the model vector space.
- `[TopologicalSpace H]`: $H$ is the model space, embedded in $E$ by the model with corners $I$.
- `[TopologicalSpace M] [ChartedSpace H M] [T2Space M] [IsManifold I (↑⊤) M]`: $M$ is a Hausdorff $C^\infty$ manifold modelled on $I$.
- `[Bundle.RiemannianBundle fun (x : M) => TangentSpace I x] [IsContMDiffRiemannianBundle I (↑⊤) E fun (x : M) => TangentSpace I x]`: each tangent space $T_yM$ carries an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, varying smoothly with $y$: a Riemannian metric.
- `[cov.ContMDiffCovariantDerivative ↑⊤]`: the implicit `cov`, written $\nabla$, is a $C^\infty$ connection on the tangent bundle.
- `(hcov : cov.IsMetricCompatible)`: $\nabla$ is compatible with the metric, $X\langle A,B\rangle = \langle\nabla_X A,B\rangle + \langle A,\nabla_X B\rangle$. No torsion condition is assumed.
- `(hκ : ∀ᶠ (y : M) in nhds x, ∀ (w u v : TangentSpace I y), (((cov.curvatureTensor y) w) u) v = κ y • (inner ℝ u v • w - inner ℝ w v • u))`: at every $y$ in some neighbourhood of $x$, $R_y(w,u)v = \kappa(y)(\langle u,v\rangle w - \langle w,v\rangle u)$ for all $w, u, v \in T_yM$.
- `(hX : ContMDiff I I.tangent ↑⊤ fun (x : M) => ⟨x, X x⟩)`: $X$ is a smooth vector field.
- `(hY : ContMDiff I I.tangent ↑⊤ fun (x : M) => ⟨x, Y x⟩)`, `(hZ : ContMDiff I I.tangent ↑⊤ fun (x : M) => ⟨x, Z x⟩)`, `(hσ : ContMDiff I I.tangent ↑⊤ fun (x : M) => ⟨x, σ x⟩)`: so are $Y$, $Z$ and σ.
- `(hκx : MDiffAt κ x)`: $\kappa : M \to \mathbb{R}$ is differentiable at $x$.
- The conclusion: at $x$, $\nabla_X(R(Y,Z)\sigma) - R(\nabla_X Y, Z)\sigma - R(Y,\nabla_X Z)\sigma - R(Y,Z)\nabla_X\sigma$, which is $(\nabla_X R)(Y,Z)\sigma$, equals $d\kappa_x(X_x)\,(\langle Z,\sigma\rangle Y - \langle Y,\sigma\rangle Z)$.

This is the standard computation behind Schur's theorem. Near $x$, $R(Y,Z)\sigma = \kappa P$ with $P = \langle Z,\sigma\rangle Y - \langle Y,\sigma\rangle Z$; the Leibniz rule splits off $d\kappa(X)P$, and metric compatibility makes $\kappa\nabla_X P$ cancel the three correction terms. With the curvature operator's sign convention (Lee's, as its docstring says), the form in `hκ` is that of sectional curvature $\kappa(y)$ at $y$.

For a graded commutative ring $A = \bigoplus_{d \ge 0} A_d$, the twisting sheaf $\mathcal{O}(0)$ on $X = \operatorname{Proj} A$ is isomorphic, as a sheaf of $\mathcal{O}_X$-modules, to the structure sheaf $\mathcal{O}_X$ regarded as a module over itself. This definition is that isomorphism.

- `[CommRing A] [SetLike σ A] [AddSubgroupClass σ A]`: $A$ is a commutative ring with a $1$, and $\sigma$ is a type of additive subgroups of $A$, from which the graded pieces are taken.
- `(𝒜 : ℕ → σ)`: the family $d \mapsto A_d$ of graded pieces, indexed by the natural numbers.
- `[GradedRing 𝒜]`: this family grades $A$: $A = \bigoplus_d A_d$ and $A_d A_e \subseteq A_{d+e}$.
- Its type, `SheafOfModules.unit (Proj 𝒜).ringCatSheaf ≅ twistingSheaf 𝒜 0`: an isomorphism of sheaves of modules over the structure sheaf of $\operatorname{Proj} A$, from the free module of rank one on it, $\mathcal{O}_X$ itself, to $\mathcal{O}(0)$.

Its value: over each open set $U$, a section of $\mathcal{O}_X$ is a function with values $a(x)$ in the homogeneous localizations $A_{(x)}$, and a section of $\mathcal{O}(0)$ is a function with values in the localizations $A_x$ that is locally a fraction of degree $0$. These isomorphisms commute with restriction, so they form an isomorphism of presheaves of modules (`PresheafOfModules.isoMk`). This is the standard identification of $\mathcal{O}(0)$ with the structure sheaf, made by the canonical comparison maps.

## What it says
A henselian pair is its own henselization: if $(R, I)$ is henselian, the structure map from $R$ to its henselization $R^h$ along $I$ is an isomorphism, and this is the inverse isomorphism $R^h \to R$ of $R$-algebras.

- `(I : Ideal R)`: an ideal $I$ of $R$.
- `[HenselianRing R I]`: $(R, I)$ is a henselian pair: $I$ lies in the Jacobson radical of $R$, and a simple root modulo $I$ of a monic polynomial over $R$ lifts to a root in $R$.
- The type: `↑(algebra I) ≃ₐ[R] R`, an isomorphism of $R$-algebras from the henselization `algebra I` of $(R, I)$, built as the filtered colimit of its étale neighbourhoods, to $R$.

The value has two maps. Forward, `lift`: the map from $R^h$ to a henselian pair given by the universal property, here to $(R, I)$ itself, which applies since $IR \subseteq I$. Backward, `Algebra.ofId`: the structure map $R \to R^h$. The composite $R \to R^h \to R$ is the identity, as the only map of $R$-algebras from $R$ to $R$; the composite $R^h \to R \to R^h$ is the identity by the uniqueness of maps out of $R^h$, since $IR^h$ lies in the Jacobson radical of $R^h$.

This is the standard consequence of the universal property of the henselization.

## What it says
Let $R^h$ be the henselization of $(R, I)$, let $(S, J)$ be a henselian pair receiving a map of pairs from $(R, I)$, and let $B$ be an étale neighbourhood of $(R, I)$. Then every $R$-algebra map $\varphi : B \to S$ is the canonical map $B \to R^h$ followed by `lift hIJ`. So there is exactly one $R$-algebra map $B \to S$.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring with a $1$; $I$ is an ideal of $R$.
- `[CommRing S] [Algebra R S]`: $S$ is a commutative ring with an $R$-algebra structure, given by the ring map `algebraMap R S`; $J$ is an ideal of $S$.
- `[HenselianRing S J]`: $(S, J)$ is a henselian pair: $J$ lies in the Jacobson radical of $S$, and a monic polynomial over $S$ with a simple root modulo $J$ has a root in $S$ lifting it.
- `(hIJ : Ideal.map (algebraMap R S) I ≤ J)`: the ideal $IS$ generated by the image of $I$ is contained in $J$.
- `(B : Neighbourhood I)`: an étale neighbourhood $B$ of $(R, I)$, an étale $R$-algebra for which $R/I \to B/IB$ is an isomorphism.
- `(φ : ↑B.obj →ₐ[R] S)`: any $R$-algebra map $\varphi$ from $B$ to $S$.
- The conclusion: `(lift hIJ).comp (stage I B) = φ`, where `stage I B` is the canonical map from $B$ into the colimit $R^h$.

It holds because two $R$-algebra maps $B \to S$ agree modulo $IS$, since $B/IB$ is the image of $R/I$; and $IS$ lies in $J$, hence in the Jacobson radical of $S$, and two maps out of an étale algebra that agree modulo an ideal inside the Jacobson radical are equal. So this is a uniqueness statement: the restriction of `lift hIJ` to the stage $B$ is the only $R$-algebra map $B \to S$.

## What it says
Let $R^h$ be the henselization of the pair $(R, I)$ and $T$ a commutative ring. Two ring maps $g_1, g_2 : R^h \to T$ that agree on (the image of) $R$ are equal, provided the ideal of $T$ generated by the image of $I$ lies in the Jacobson radical of $T$.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring with a $1$; $I$ is an ideal of $R$.
- `[CommRing T]`: $T$ is a commutative ring with a $1$; $g_1$ and $g_2$ are ring maps from `algebra I`, the henselization, to $T$.
- `(h : g₁.comp (algebraMap R ↑(algebra I)) = g₂.comp (algebraMap R ↑(algebra I)))`: $g_1$ and $g_2$ agree after composing with the structure map $R \to R^h$, that is, on the image of $R$.
- `(hI : Ideal.map (g₁.comp (algebraMap R ↑(algebra I))) I ≤ ⊥.jacobson)`: the ideal $IT$ generated by the image of $I$ under the composite $R \to R^h \to T$ is contained in the Jacobson radical of $T$, the intersection of its maximal ideals.
- The conclusion: $g_1 = g_2$.

This is the version for ring maps of the statement for $R$-algebra maps: making $T$ an $R$-algebra through the common composite $R \to T$ turns $g_1$ and $g_2$ into $R$-algebra maps, which are then equal. It is the uniqueness part of the universal property of the henselization, with the hypothesis that $IT$ lies in the Jacobson radical in place of a henselian target.

## What it says
In a finitely generated algebra $A$ over a field $k$ whose spectrum is irreducible, every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ has height equal to the Krull dimension of $A$.

- `[Field k]`: $k$ is a field.
- `[CommRing A] [Algebra k A]`: $A$ is a commutative ring with a $k$-algebra structure.
- `[Algebra.FiniteType k A]`: $A$ is finitely generated as a $k$-algebra, a quotient of a polynomial ring over $k$ in finitely many variables.
- `[IrreducibleSpace (PrimeSpectrum A)]`: $\operatorname{Spec} A$, with its Zariski topology, is irreducible: nonempty and not the union of two proper closed subsets. Equivalently, $A$ has exactly one minimal prime ideal.
- `(m : Ideal A)`: an ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $A$.
- `[m.IsMaximal]`: $\mathfrak m$ is a maximal ideal.
- The conclusion: `m.height`, the height of $\mathfrak m$, the supremum of the lengths $n$ of chains of primes $\mathfrak p_0 \subsetneq \dots \subsetneq \mathfrak p_n = \mathfrak m$, equals `ringKrullDim A`, the Krull dimension of $A$.

This is the standard fact that the closed points of an irreducible affine variety $X$ all have local dimension $\dim X$. It follows from the dimension formula $\operatorname{ht} \mathfrak p + \dim A/\mathfrak p = \dim A$ for a finitely generated domain over a field, applied to $A$ modulo its nilradical, since $\dim A/\mathfrak m = 0$. Finite type is needed: $k[x]_{(x)}[y]$ is a domain of dimension $2$, not of finite type over $k$, and its maximal ideal $(xy - 1)$ has height $1$.

## What it says
A Noetherian ring $R$ is reduced if and only if it satisfies Serre's conditions $(R_0)$ and $(S_1)$: its localizations at minimal primes are fields, and it has no embedded primes.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring with a $1$.
- `[IsNoetherianRing R]`: $R$ is Noetherian: every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated.
- The conclusion: `IsReduced R`, that $R$ has no nonzero nilpotent elements, holds if and only if both
  - `Ring.SatisfiesSerreR 0 R`, condition $(R_0)$: for every prime $\mathfrak p$ of height $0$, that is every minimal prime, the local ring $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is regular, which in dimension $0$ means that it is a field; and
  - `Module.SatisfiesSerreS 1 R R`, condition $(S_1)$ for $R$ as a module over itself: for every prime $\mathfrak p$, $\operatorname{depth} R_{\mathfrak p} \ge \min(1, \dim R_{\mathfrak p})$. So every prime that is not minimal contains a nonzerodivisor after localizing, and no associated prime of $R$ is embedded.

This is the lemma of the Stacks Project as stated there, for the same rings, Noetherian ones, with the same definitions of $(R_k)$ and of $(S_k)$ as a bound on depth by $\min(k, \dim \operatorname{Supp} M_{\mathfrak p})$.

## What it says
If a commutative ring $A$ contains a copy of a polynomial ring $k[X_i : i \in \iota]$ in finitely many variables over a field $k$, and is integral over it, then the Krull dimension of $A$ is the number of variables $|\iota|$.

- `[Field k]`: $k$ is a field.
- `[Finite ι]`: the index set $\iota$ of the variables is finite.
- `[CommRing A]`: $A$ is a commutative ring with a $1$.
- `(g : MvPolynomial ι k →+* A)`: a ring map $g$ from the polynomial ring $k[X_i : i \in \iota]$ to $A$.
- `(hinj : Function.Injective ⇑g)`: $g$ is injective, so $A$ contains a copy of the polynomial ring.
- `(hint : g.IsIntegral)`: $g$ is integral: every element of $A$ is a root of a monic polynomial whose coefficients lie in the image of $g$.
- The conclusion: `ringKrullDim A = ↑(Nat.card ι)`, the Krull dimension of $A$ is $|\iota|$.

This is the standard dimension count. An injective integral extension has the same Krull dimension as its base, by lying over, going up and incomparability, and $k[X_1, \dots, X_n]$ has dimension $n$. With Noether normalization it gives the dimension of any finitely generated algebra over a field. Both hypotheses on $g$ are needed: $k[X] \subset k[X, Y]$ is injective but not integral, with dimensions $1$ and $2$. The map $g$ is only a ring map, so $A$ need not be given a $k$-algebra structure beforehand.

## What it says
A finitely generated domain $A$ over a field $k$ has Krull dimension equal to the transcendence degree over $k$ of its fraction field $K$.

- `[Field k]`: $k$ is a field.
- `[CommRing A] [Algebra k A]`: $A$ is a commutative ring with a $k$-algebra structure.
- `[Algebra.FiniteType k A]`: $A$ is finitely generated as a $k$-algebra.
- `[Field K] [Algebra A K]`: $K$ is a field with a ring map from $A$.
- `[Algebra k K] [IsScalarTower k A K]`: $K$ is also a $k$-algebra, and its map from $k$ is the composite $k \to A \to K$.
- `[IsFractionRing A K]`: $K$ is the ring of fractions of $A$, the localization of $A$ at its nonzerodivisors. As $K$ is a field, $A$ embeds into it and is a domain, with fraction field $K$.
- The conclusion: `ringKrullDim A = ↑(Cardinal.toNat (Algebra.trdeg k K))`, the Krull dimension of $A$ is $\operatorname{trdeg}_k K$.

This is the classical theorem as stated in the literature, for the same rings: domains of finite type over a field. The domain hypothesis is not written out, but it follows from $A$ having a field of fractions.

## What it says
For a finitely generated algebra $A$ over a field $k$ and a point $\mathfrak p$ of $\operatorname{Spec} A$, the local dimension of $\operatorname{Spec} A$ at $\mathfrak p$ is $\operatorname{ht} \mathfrak p + \dim A/\mathfrak p$.

- `[Field k]`: $k$ is a field.
- `[CommRing A] [Algebra k A]`: $A$ is a commutative ring with a $k$-algebra structure.
- `[Algebra.FiniteType k A]`: $A$ is finitely generated as a $k$-algebra.
- `(p : PrimeSpectrum A)`: a point $\mathfrak p$ of $\operatorname{Spec} A$, that is a prime ideal `p.asIdeal` of $A$.
- The conclusion: `topologicalKrullDimAt (PrimeSpectrum A) p`, the local dimension of $\operatorname{Spec} A$ at $\mathfrak p$, the smallest dimension of an open neighbourhood of $\mathfrak p$, equals `↑p.asIdeal.height + ringKrullDim (A ⧸ p.asIdeal)`, the height of $\mathfrak p$ plus the Krull dimension of $A/\mathfrak p$.

No irreducibility is assumed. Near $\mathfrak p$ only the irreducible components $V(\mathfrak q)$ through $\mathfrak p$ count, for the minimal primes $\mathfrak q \subseteq \mathfrak p$. Each has dimension $\dim A/\mathfrak q = \operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p/\mathfrak q) + \dim A/\mathfrak p$ by the dimension formula for finitely generated domains over a field, and the largest $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p/\mathfrak q)$ is $\operatorname{ht} \mathfrak p$. In $k[x,y,z]/(xz, yz)$, a plane and a line through the origin, both sides are $1$ at a closed point of the line off the plane, and $2$ at the origin.

## What it says
For a finitely generated algebra $A$ over a field $k$ and a point $\mathfrak p$ of $X = \operatorname{Spec} A$, the local dimension of $X$ at $\mathfrak p$ is $\dim A_{\mathfrak p} + \operatorname{trdeg}_k \kappa(\mathfrak p)$, where $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is the local ring at $\mathfrak p$ and $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ its residue field.

- `[Field k]`: $k$ is a field.
- `[CommRing A] [Algebra k A]`: $A$ is a commutative ring with a $k$-algebra structure.
- `[Algebra.FiniteType k A]`: $A$ is finitely generated as a $k$-algebra.
- `(p : PrimeSpectrum A)`: a point $\mathfrak p$ of $\operatorname{Spec} A$, that is a prime ideal `p.asIdeal` of $A$.
- The conclusion: `topologicalKrullDimAt (PrimeSpectrum A) p`, the smallest dimension of an open neighbourhood of $\mathfrak p$ in $\operatorname{Spec} A$, equals the Krull dimension of `Localization.AtPrime p.asIdeal`, the local ring $A_{\mathfrak p}$, plus the transcendence degree over $k$ of `p.asIdeal.ResidueField`, the residue field $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$.

This is the standard formula for the local dimension of a scheme of finite type over a field, with no irreducibility assumed. It is the height formula $\operatorname{ht} \mathfrak p + \dim A/\mathfrak p$ rewritten, since $\dim A_{\mathfrak p} = \operatorname{ht} \mathfrak p$, and $\dim A/\mathfrak p = \operatorname{trdeg}_k \kappa(\mathfrak p)$ as $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ is the fraction field of $A/\mathfrak p$. At the generic point of the affine line both sides are $1 = 0 + 1$.

## What it says
The Demazure operator $D_i$ of a root $\alpha_i$ is idempotent: $D_i(D_i f) = D_i f$ for every $f$ in the group ring $\mathbb{Z}[M]$.

- `[AddCommGroup M] [AddCommGroup N]`: $M$ and $N$ are abelian groups, playing the roles of the weight and coweight lattices.
- `(P : RootPairing ι ℤ M N)`: a root pairing over $\mathbb{Z}$: roots $\alpha_j \in M$ and coroots $\alpha_j^\vee \in N$ indexed by $\iota$, with a perfect pairing $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle : M \times N \to \mathbb{Z}$ such that $\langle \alpha_j, \alpha_j^\vee \rangle = 2$ and the reflections $s_j(x) = x - \langle x, \alpha_j^\vee \rangle \alpha_j$ permute the roots, and dually for the coroots.
- `(i : ι)`: an index $i$, picking the root $\alpha_i$.
- `(f : AddMonoidAlgebra ℤ M)`: an element $f$ of $\mathbb{Z}[M]$, a finite integer combination of formal exponentials $e^x$, $x \in M$.
- The conclusion: applying `P.demazureOperator i` twice to $f$ gives the same as applying it once.

Here $D_i$ is the integral Demazure operator: the $\mathbb{Z}$-linear map of $\mathbb{Z}[M]$ sending $e^x$, with $m = \langle x, \alpha_i^\vee \rangle$, to $e^x + e^{x - \alpha_i} + \dots + e^{x - m\alpha_i}$ when $m \ge 0$, so that $(1 - e^{-\alpha_i}) D_i f = f - e^{-\alpha_i} s_i f$. Idempotence is the standard property of Demazure's operators. It holds because every value of $D_i$ is $s_i$-invariant and $D_i$ fixes the $s_i$-invariant elements.

## What it says
The localization identity characterizes the Demazure operator: $D_i f$ is the unique $g$ in $\mathbb{Z}[M]$ with $(1 - e^{-\alpha_i})\, g = f - e^{-\alpha_i}\, s_i(f)$.

- `[AddCommGroup M] [AddCommGroup N]`: $M$ and $N$ are abelian groups, playing the roles of the weight and coweight lattices.
- `(P : RootPairing ι ℤ M N)`: a root pairing over $\mathbb{Z}$: roots $\alpha_j \in M$ and coroots $\alpha_j^\vee \in N$ indexed by $\iota$, with a perfect pairing $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle : M \times N \to \mathbb{Z}$ such that $\langle \alpha_j, \alpha_j^\vee \rangle = 2$ and the reflections $s_j(x) = x - \langle x, \alpha_j^\vee \rangle \alpha_j$ permute the roots, and dually for the coroots.
- `(i : ι)`: an index $i$, picking the root $\alpha_i$ (`P.root i`).
- The conclusion, for any $f, g \in \mathbb{Z}[M]$: `(P.demazureOperator i) f = g` holds if and only if $(1 - e^{-\alpha_i})\, g = f - e^{-\alpha_i}\, s_i(f)$. Here `AddMonoidAlgebra.single (-P.root i) 1` is the exponential $e^{-\alpha_i}$, and `AddMonoidAlgebra.mapDomainRingEquiv ℤ (P.reflection i).toAddEquiv` is the ring automorphism $s_i$ of $\mathbb{Z}[M]$ with $e^x \mapsto e^{s_i x}$.

This is the usual description of Demazure's operator as a quotient, $D_i f = (f - e^{-\alpha_i} s_i f)/(1 - e^{-\alpha_i})$. The division is exact in $\mathbb{Z}[M]$, and its result is unique because $1 - e^{-\alpha_i}$ is not a zero divisor: $\alpha_i$ has infinite order, since $\langle \alpha_i, \alpha_i^\vee \rangle = 2$, so multiplication by $e^{-\alpha_i}$ fixes no nonzero finitely supported element.

- `(P : RootPairing ι ℤ M N)`: a root pairing over $\mathbb{Z}$: a perfect pairing $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ of $M$ and $N$ into $\mathbb{Z}$, with roots $\alpha_i \in M$ and coroots $\alpha_i^\vee \in N$ indexed by $\iota$, such that $\langle \alpha_i, \alpha_i^\vee \rangle = 2$ and the reflections permute the roots and the coroots.
- `(i : ι)`: an index, which picks the root $\alpha_i$ (`P.root i`), its coroot and the reflection $s_i(x) = x - \langle x, \alpha_i^\vee\rangle \alpha_i$ of $M$ (`P.reflection i`).
- `(f : AddMonoidAlgebra ℤ M)`: an element $f$ of $\mathbb{Z}[M]$, a finite $\mathbb{Z}$-linear combination of the basis elements $e^x$, $x \in M$.
- The conclusion: `AddMonoidAlgebra.single (-P.root i) 1` is $e^{-\alpha_i}$, `P.demazureOperator i f` is $D_i(f)$, and `AddMonoidAlgebra.mapDomainRingEquiv ℤ (P.reflection i).toAddEquiv f` is $s_i(f)$; the equation is $(1 - e^{-\alpha_i}) D_i(f) = f - e^{-\alpha_i} s_i(f)$.

On a basis element it is the telescoping of the finite $\alpha_i$-string that $D_i$ gives against $1 - e^{-\alpha_i}$: for $\langle x, \alpha_i^\vee\rangle = m \ge 0$, both sides are $e^x - e^{x-(m+1)\alpha_i}$. Since $\alpha_i$ has infinite order in $M$ (its pairing with $\alpha_i^\vee$ is $2$), $1 - e^{-\alpha_i}$ is not a zero divisor of $\mathbb{Z}[M]$, so the identity determines $D_i$: it is the classical quotient formula $D_i(e^x) = (e^x - e^{-\alpha_i} e^{s_i x})/(1 - e^{-\alpha_i})$ of the docstring.

- `[Field 𝕜] [LinearOrder 𝕜]`: $\Bbbk$ is a field with a linear order; no compatibility between the two is asked.
- `[AddCommGroup V] [Module 𝕜 V]`: $V$ is a vector space over $\Bbbk$.
- The implicit $f$ is a linear functional $V \to \Bbbk$, an element of `Module.Dual 𝕜 V`, which measures heights, and the implicit $x \in V$ is the vector by which paths are lowered; they play the parts of the coroot $\alpha^\vee$ and of the root $\alpha$.
- `(l : List V)`: a list $[v_1, \dots, v_m]$ of vectors, the successive segments of a path from $0$.
- The conclusion: with $h$ = `listMinHeight f l`, the minimal height of the path, `listLower f x l` is `some (reflectRecords f x (h + 1) l)` when $1 \le f(v_1 + \dots + v_m) - h$, and `none` otherwise.

So the operator is defined exactly when the final height exceeds the minimal height $h$ by at least $1$. It then applies `reflectRecords` with the cap $h + 1$: this reflects, by `Module.preReflection x f`, that is $v \mapsto v - f(v)\,x$, pieces of the path chosen by its running height, starting from $0$, and that cap. These are the domain and the shape of Littelmann's lowering operator $f_\alpha$, which gives $0$ when the final height exceeds the minimum by less than $1$.

## What it says
The minimal height of a piecewise-linear path given by its list of segments, computed by a recursion along the list.

- `[Semiring 𝕜] [LinearOrder 𝕜]`: $\Bbbk$ is a semiring with a linear order; no compatibility between the two is asked.
- `[AddCommMonoid V] [Module 𝕜 V]`: $V$ is a module over $\Bbbk$, an additive commutative monoid with a scalar multiplication by $\Bbbk$.
- `(f : Module.Dual 𝕜 V)`: a linear functional $f : V \to \Bbbk$; $f(p)$ is the height of the point $p$.
- The result is a function `List V → 𝕜`, from lists $[v_1, \dots, v_n]$ of vectors, the successive segments of a path from $0$, to scalars.

Its value is given by the recursion $m([\,]) = 0$ and $m(v :: l) = \min(0, f(v) + m(l))$: the start, at height $0$, or the minimum over the rest of the path shifted by the height $f(v)$ of the first segment. When addition preserves the order, this is the minimum of $f$ over the vertices $0, v_1, v_1 + v_2, \dots, v_1 + \dots + v_n$, the starting vertex included. Over an ordered field the height is affine on each segment, so this is the minimum of the height over the whole path, the number $m_\alpha$ in Littelmann's root operators, with $f$ the coroot.

The embedding of an exact category $C$ into its idempotent completion is exact: it sends every conflation of $C$ to a conflation of the exact structure induced on the idempotent completion.

- `[CategoryTheory.Category.{v, u} C]`: $C$ is a category, with objects in universe `u` and morphisms in universe `v`.
- `[CategoryTheory.Preadditive C] [CategoryTheory.Limits.HasZeroObject C] [CategoryTheory.Limits.HasBinaryBiproducts C]`: $C$ is additive. Its morphisms form abelian groups with bilinear composition, and it has a zero object and binary direct sums.
- `(E : ExactStructure C)`: a Quillen exact structure on $C$, given by its docstring in a self-dual presentation: a class of conflations, the kernel-cokernel pairs $X \to Y \to Z$ called short exact sequences, satisfying Quillen's axioms.

This functor goes from $C$ to its idempotent completion `Karoubi C` and sends $X$ to $X$ with its identity.

The idempotent completion `Karoubi C` has as objects the pairs $(X, p)$ of an object and an idempotent $p : X \to X$, and as morphisms $(X, p) \to (Y, q)$ the $f : X \to Y$ with $f = q f p$. A conflation-exact functor is an additive functor that maps conflations to conflations, which is the usual notion of an exact functor between exact categories. The statement is the standard fact that the inclusion of an exact category into its idempotent completion preserves exactness.

## What it says
For a non-zero-divisor $w$ of a commutative ring $S$, the stable cokernel functor $\mathrm{HMF}(S, w) \to \underline{\mathrm{Gproj}}(S/(w))$ is fully faithful: on every set of morphisms it is a bijection.

- `[CommRing S]`: $S$ is a commutative ring, and $w \in S$ (implicit) is the potential.
- `(hw : w ∈ nonZeroDivisors S)`: $w$ is a non-zero-divisor of $S$: $s w = 0$ implies $s = 0$.
- The conclusion: `(quotientGorensteinProjectiveStableCokernel hw).FullyFaithful`. The functor goes from the homotopy category of finite-projective matrix factorizations of $w$ to the stable category of finitely generated Gorenstein-projective modules over the hypersurface $S/(w)$, and it is full and faithful.

A finite-projective matrix factorization of $w$ is a pair of finitely generated projective $S$-modules $P_0, P_1$ with maps $d_0 : P_0 \to P_1$ and $d_1 : P_1 \to P_0$ whose composites are multiplication by $w$. In the homotopy category, morphisms are taken modulo those that are null-homotopic. The functor sends a matrix factorization to the cokernel of its reduction modulo $w$, a Gorenstein-projective $S/(w)$-module. The stable category is the quotient of finitely generated Gorenstein-projective modules by the morphisms that factor through a projective object, for the exact structure induced from all modules. The value assembles the structure from the separate facts that the functor is full and that it is faithful.

This is the standard correspondence between matrix factorizations and modules over the hypersurface, of which only full faithfulness is claimed here; essential surjectivity is not part of it. The statement holds for every commutative ring, with no regularity or locality assumed.

## What it says
A nonempty scheme $X$ smooth over a field $k$ has a point with values in some finite separable extension $K$ of $k$: a morphism $\mathrm{Spec}\, K \to X$ over $\mathrm{Spec}\, k$.

- `(f : X ⟶ Spec ↧k)`: a morphism of schemes from a scheme $X$ (implicit) to $\mathrm{Spec}\, k$, which makes $X$ a scheme over $k$.
- `[Smooth f]`: $f$ is smooth: over affine opens, the induced maps of rings of sections are smooth ring maps.
- `[Nonempty ↥X]`: $X$ has at least one point.
- The conclusion: there are a field $K$ and a $k$-algebra structure on it such that $K$ is finite-dimensional over $k$ (`Module.Finite k K`) and separable over $k$ (`Algebra.IsSeparable k K`), together with a morphism of schemes $g : \mathrm{Spec}\, K \to X$ with $f \circ g$ equal to $\mathrm{Spec}$ of the inclusion $k \to K$. In other words, $g$ is a $K$-point of $X$ over $k$.

This is the standard consequence of the density of closed points with separable residue field in a scheme smooth over $k$. A closed point $x$ of a scheme locally of finite type over $k$ has a residue field $\kappa(x)$ finite over $k$, and when $\kappa(x)$ is separable, $K = \kappa(x)$ and the canonical morphism $\mathrm{Spec}\, \kappa(x) \to X$ give the statement.

## What it says
For a quasi-coherent sheaf $\mathcal{A} = \bigoplus_n \mathcal{A}_n$ of $\mathbb{N}$-graded commutative $\mathcal{O}_X$-algebras on a scheme $X$, the charts of its relative Proj fit into cartesian squares. For affine opens $U$, the projections $\mathrm{Proj}(\bigoplus_n \Gamma(U, \mathcal{A}_n)) \to \mathrm{Spec}\, \Gamma(X, U)$ form a natural transformation every one of whose naturality squares is cartesian.

- `(A : CommMon (GradedObject ℕ X.Modules))`: a commutative monoid object in $\mathbb{N}$-graded sheaves of $\mathcal{O}_X$-modules on a scheme $X$ (implicit), that is, a sheaf of $\mathbb{N}$-graded commutative $\mathcal{O}_X$-algebras. Its degree-$n$ piece is `A.X n`.
- `[∀ (n : ℕ), SheafOfModules.IsQuasicoherent (A.X n)]`: every graded piece $\mathcal{A}_n$ is quasi-coherent.
- The conclusion: `NatTrans.Equifibered A.relativeProjToSpec`. Here `A.relativeProjToSpec` is the natural transformation from $U \mapsto \mathrm{Proj}(\bigoplus_n \Gamma(U, \mathcal{A}_n))$ to $U \mapsto \mathrm{Spec}\, \Gamma(X, U)$ on the affine Zariski site of $X$, whose arrows are, by its docstring, basic opens $D(f) \to U$. Being equifibered means that for every such arrow the square
  $$\mathrm{Proj}(\textstyle\bigoplus_n \Gamma(D(f), \mathcal{A}_n)) \to \mathrm{Proj}(\textstyle\bigoplus_n \Gamma(U, \mathcal{A}_n))$$
  over $\mathrm{Spec}\, \Gamma(X, D(f)) \to \mathrm{Spec}\, \Gamma(X, U)$ is a pullback.

This is the base-change property of Proj that underlies relative Proj. Because each $\mathcal{A}_n$ is quasi-coherent, its sections over $D(f)$ are the localization at $f$ of its sections over $U$, and Proj of the localized graded ring is the fibre product of the Proj over $U$ with $D(f)$.

## What it says

## What it says
If $k$ is a field, $K$ is a Noetherian $k$-algebra and $A$ is a finitely generated $k$-algebra, then
$$\dim(K \otimes_k A) = \dim K + \dim A,$$
where $\dim$ is the Krull dimension.

- `[Field k]`: $k$ (an implicit argument) is a field.
- `[CommRing K] [IsNoetherianRing K] [Algebra k K]`: $K$ is a commutative Noetherian ring, every ideal finitely generated, with a $k$-algebra structure. It need not be a field, despite its letter.
- `[CommRing A] [Algebra k A] [Algebra.FiniteType k A]`: $A$ is a commutative ring with a $1$ that is a finitely generated $k$-algebra.
- The conclusion: `ringKrullDim (TensorProduct k K A) = ringKrullDim K + ringKrullDim A`, the Krull dimension of the ring $K \otimes_k A$ is the sum of those of $K$ and $A$.

This extends the standard formula $\dim K[x_1, \dots, x_n] = \dim K + n$ for a Noetherian ring $K$, which is the case $A = k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$, to every finitely generated $A$; the case of a field $K$, of dimension $0$, says that extending the base field does not change the dimension. By Noether normalization $A$ is finite over a polynomial ring $k[x_1, \dots, x_d]$ with $d = \dim A$, into which it embeds, and $K \otimes_k A$ is then finite over $K[x_1, \dots, x_d]$, into which it embeds, $K$ being flat over the field $k$.

- `(hZ : IsIrreducible Z)`: $Z$ is irreducible: nonempty, and not the union of two closed subsets of it other than itself.
- `(hZc : IsClosed Z)`: $Z$ is closed, so $Z = V(\mathfrak p)$ for a prime $\mathfrak p$ of $A$.
- `(hU : IsOpen U)`: $U$ is open.
- `(hZU : (Z ∩ U).Nonempty)`: $U$ meets $Z$.

This is the standard fact that a nonempty open subset of an irreducible variety has the variety's dimension, here for $Z \cong \operatorname{Spec}(A/\mathfrak p)$ and its open subset $Z \cap U$. Each hypothesis is needed: with $Z$ the generic point and one closed point of the affine line (irreducible, not closed, of dimension $1$) and $U$ the complement of that closed point, $Z \cap U$ is a single point; a line together with a point, or a closed point as $U$, fail likewise.

## What it says
The density of the generalized normal law (also called the exponential power law) with location $m$, scale $s$ and shape $p$, as a real-valued function of $x$:
$$f(x) = \frac{p}{2s\,\Gamma(1/p)}\exp\Bigl(-\Bigl|\frac{x-m}{s}\Bigr|^p\Bigr) \quad \text{when } s > 0 \text{ and } p > 0,$$
and $f(x) = 0$ otherwise.

- `(m s p x : ℝ)`: four real numbers: the location `m`, the scale `s`, the shape `p`, and the point `x` at which the density is evaluated.
- The value: when $0 < s$ and $0 < p$, `p / (2 * s * Real.Gamma p⁻¹) * Real.exp (-|(x - m) / s| ^ p)`, which is the formula above, with `Real.Gamma` the Gamma function and `Real.exp` the exponential. In every other case the value is $0$.

This is the usual form of the generalized normal density for $s > 0$ and $p > 0$. The constant makes the total mass $1$: the substitution $u = |(x-m)/s|^p$ gives $\int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-|(x-m)/s|^p}\,dx = \frac{2s}{p}\,\Gamma(1/p)$. At $p = 1$ the formula is the Laplace density $\frac{1}{2s}e^{-|x-m|/s}$. At $p = 2$ it is $\frac{1}{s\sqrt{\pi}}e^{-(x-m)^2/s^2}$, the normal density with mean $m$ and variance $s^2/2$.

## What it says
If a real random variable $X$ has the Lévy law with location $m$ and scale $c$, and $b > 0$, then $a + bX$ has the Lévy law with location $a + bm$ and scale $bc$, for every real $a$.

- `[MeasurableSpace Ω]`: a σ-algebra on the sample space $\Omega$, a type, which makes it a measurable space. The measure $P$ on $\Omega$ and the function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ are implicit arguments.
- `(hb : 0 < b)`: the real number $b$, the factor, is positive.
- `(a : ℝ)`: a real number $a$, the shift, arbitrary.
- `(hX : ProbabilityTheory.HasLaw X (levyMeasure m c) P)`: under $P$, the random variable $X$ has law `levyMeasure m c`, the Lévy law with location $m$ and scale $c$. That is, the image of $P$ under $X$ is that law.
- The conclusion: `ProbabilityTheory.HasLaw (fun (ω : Ω) => a + b * X ω) (levyMeasure (a + b * m) (b * c)) P`. Under $P$, the random variable $\omega \mapsto a + b\,X(\omega)$ has the Lévy law with location $a + bm$ and scale $bc$.

This is the location-scale property of the Lévy law. By its docstring, `levyMeasure m c` is the inverse-gamma law of shape $1/2$ and scale $c/2$, translated by $m$. Multiplying by $b > 0$ multiplies an inverse-gamma scale by $b$ and the translation by $b$, and adding $a$ moves the location by $a$. The hypothesis $b > 0$ is the right one. For $b < 0$ the image is a reflected Lévy law, carried by a half-line to the left, and for $b = 0$ it is the point mass at $a$, neither of which is a Lévy law.

## What it says
If $Z$ is a standard Gaussian random variable and $V$ an independent chi-squared random variable with $\nu > 0$ degrees of freedom, then $(Z + \delta)/\sqrt{V/\nu}$ has the noncentral t law with $\nu$ degrees of freedom and noncentrality $\delta$.

Here $\Omega$ is the sample space, with a σ-algebra and a measure $P$, and $Z, V : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ are random variables. The parameters $\nu$ and $\delta$ are real numbers. All of these are implicit arguments.

- `(hν : 0 < ν)`: the number of degrees of freedom $\nu$ is positive. It is a real number, not necessarily an integer.
- `(hZV : ProbabilityTheory.IndepFun Z V P)`: $Z$ and $V$ are independent under $P$.
- `(hZ : ProbabilityTheory.HasLaw Z (ProbabilityTheory.gaussianReal 0 1) P)`: under $P$, $Z$ has the Gaussian law with mean $0$ and variance $1$.
- `(hV : ProbabilityTheory.HasLaw V (chiSquaredMeasure ν) P)`: under $P$, $V$ has the chi-squared law with $\nu$ degrees of freedom. By its docstring, for $\nu > 0$ this is the gamma law of shape $\nu/2$ and rate $1/2$.
- The conclusion: under $P$, the random variable $\omega \mapsto (Z(\omega) + \delta)/\sqrt{V(\omega)/\nu}$ has law `noncentralTMeasure ν δ`, the noncentral t law with $\nu$ degrees of freedom and noncentrality $\delta$.

This is the standard construction of the noncentral t law, in random-variable form: the noncentrality $\delta$ shifts the Gaussian numerator, and the denominator is the square root of the chi-squared variable divided by its degrees of freedom. At $\delta = 0$ it is the usual construction of Student's t law. Real degrees of freedom $\nu > 0$ are the general case of the definition.
